events.text: A clear night after the first hard frost. You wake on the river ice and the snake is very quiet, which it never is. It is looking at your back. Where the plates of your shell were black as an inkstone, there are stars: the Dipper on the first plate, the Ox and the Girl, Emptiness, Rooftop, Encampment, the Wall. The northern sky has come down and lain on you. Where an ending is written, the stars burn. Where none is, the plate is bare. Where the snake wrote something it never saw, the stars are there, but they glow wrong, a little red, like a lamp behind oiled paper.

choices.text: Lie still and let the snake read the sky off your own back

effects.log: It reads you mansion by mansion, out loud, the way it reads eddies: fast, sure, delighted. At the cracked ones it goes quieter. At the bare ones it says, "Room," as if that were good news. Perhaps it is.

choices.text: Crane round to look up at the real sky, and compare

effects.log: It takes the tortoise most of the night to get its neck round far enough. The sky above and the sky on your back match star for star, except where your back is bare, and there the real sky goes on burning without you.

choices.text: Read it together, one head the stars, one head the gaps

effects.log: The snake names the stars. The tortoise names what each one was: the drowned fisherman, the bridge, the wedding on the far bank. By dawn you have read your whole life off your own back, and neither of you has interrupted the other once.

events.text: The Dipper plate is bare: the mansion that rules how long a life is. In the house by the ford an old woman the whole valley calls Grandmother Pine has lived a hundred and four years and has decided, quite firmly, that this winter is enough. She has had her grave clothes sewn since spring. The snake looks at the stars on your back and says she has nine days. Then it looks up the mountain, toward the place where two old men play baduk over a book of names, and says nothing at all, very loudly.

choices.text: Lie under her window for nine days, and witness it

effects.log: On the ninth night she tells her great-grandchildren the story of the tortoise under the ford, gets it mostly right, and goes to sleep in the middle of a sentence. You hear the last breath. You write it as it was: a long life, finished on purpose. The Dipper plate lights on your back.

choices.text: Let the snake go up the mountain and ask for more years for her

effects.log: The snake comes back down at dawn with three more years in its mouth, very pleased. She uses them to scold everyone she ever loved, thoroughly, and dies laughing. There is nothing to write: the ending was changed. The tortoise wanted to write. It says nothing about it for a decade.

choices.text: Sleep, and let the snake write it from what the ferry says

effects.log: The ferry hands say she died in her sleep, praying. She did not pray; she was telling a story. The snake writes the ferry's version, neat and quick, and the Dipper stars come up on the plate glowing faintly wrong.

events.text: The Ox plate is bare: the mansion of roads, passes and bridges. Downriver a magistrate has built a stone bridge on nine piers, and the old rope ferry beside it will cross for the last time at the Cold Dew festival. The ferryman is eighty and has made the crossing, by his own count, two hundred and eleven thousand times. He has invited the whole county to the last one, and is sober for it.

choices.text: Hold the ferry steady from beneath, the last crossing, and watch

effects.log: You are under the hull all the way over, as you have been in every flood for a hundred years. On the far bank the ferryman cuts the rope himself and lets it go down the river, and stands there a long time. A crossing ended. The Ox plate lights.

choices.text: Crack the new bridge's ninth pier, so the ferry is still needed

effects.log: The ninth pier settles in the spring thaw and the magistrate closes the bridge for repairs that take thirty years. The ferryman crosses until he dies, delighted, never knowing why. The tortoise is appalled. The snake says a crossing is a crossing.

choices.text: Let the snake write it from the festival gossip

effects.log: The gossip says the ferryman wept and threw himself in after the rope. He did not: he went home and slept for two days. The snake writes the gossip. The Ox stars glow on the plate, slightly pink.

events.text: The Girl plate is bare: the mansion of weddings made and broken. On the near bank a bride in a red jacket sits in a palanquin at the ferry steps, waiting. On the far bank, the groom's procession, the wild goose of carved wood carried in front, the musicians. Between them, the river in spring flood, and no ferry will go out in it. The two families have been at war over a boundary stone for three generations, and both of them are quietly hoping the river wins.

choices.text: Carry the groom across on your back, and watch the wedding made

effects.log: The groom comes over on the back of a black tortoise the size of a threshing floor, still holding the wooden goose, white to the lips. The bows are made on the near bank in the mud, with both families watching and neither able to say a word. You saw it, every bow. The Girl plate lights.

choices.text: Stay under the water and watch the wedding broken

effects.log: At dusk the palanquin is carried home. The groom's musicians play one sad tune across the water and stop. The boundary stone is fought over for another hundred years. It was an ending, and you watched all of it, and the Girl plate lights, and it is not a happy light.

choices.text: Let the snake ask the river what happened, a year later

effects.log: The river says the bride drowned herself. She did not: she married a salt merchant two villages over and was very happy. The snake writes the river's version. The Girl stars glow on your back, wrong.

events.text: The Emptiness plate is bare: the mansion of mourning and weeping. On the slope above your river a son has lived three years in a straw hut beside his father's grave, in undyed hemp, eating gruel, as the old rites ask. Tomorrow the three years end. He will take down the hut, bow to the mound, and walk back into his life. Nobody else will be there. Nobody else remembers it is tomorrow.

choices.text: Climb the slope and be there when he takes the hut down

effects.log: He sees you at the edge of the grave-clearing at dawn and is not afraid. He takes the straw down bundle by bundle and bows to the mound four times, and then, after a pause, once to you. A mourning ended. The Emptiness plate lights.

choices.text: Send the snake down to the village to remind his brothers it is tomorrow

effects.log: His brothers come up at dawn with rice cakes and an argument, and the end of the mourning becomes a picnic. It is better for him. It is not the ending the snake read, and so there is nothing to write. The tortoise says nothing about this for seven years.

choices.text: Let the snake write it from the smoke of the burnt hut

effects.log: Smoke on the slope, an empty clearing. The snake writes that he burnt the hut and wept. He did not burn it; a herd boy did, a month later. The Emptiness stars come up glowing wrong.

events.text: The Rooftop plate is bare: the mansion of treasuries and of raising roofs, and of roofs that fall. A great house by the river has been sold for debt, nine generations of a scholar's family, and tomorrow the buyer's men will take down the ridge beam with the family's founding date written on its underside. The old master of the house has asked to sit in the yard and watch.

choices.text: Lie in the garden pond all night and watch the beam come down

effects.log: The beam comes down at noon on ropes. The old master stands to read the date on its underside before it goes into the cart, and reads it aloud, and sits down again. A house ended. The Rooftop plate lights, and you will never forget the date.

choices.text: Let the snake show the old master where his grandfather buried the silver

effects.log: Under the third flagstone by the well. The snake has known for sixty years. The debt is paid by evening and the beam stays where it is. There is nothing to write. The tortoise says a witness who digs is not a witness. The snake says a witness who watches a man lose his house for nothing is not a friend.

choices.text: Let the snake write it from the buyer's ledger

effects.log: The ledger says the house was bought fairly and the family left gladly. The snake writes the ledger. The Rooftop stars glow on your back like a coal in ash.

events.text: The Encampment plate is bare: the mansion of an army's granary and of great earthworks. On the northern frontier a garrison that has held the same earth wall for two hundred years is being disbanded by an order from a capital that has forgotten why the wall was built. The last soldiers are burning the camp's empty granary so that no one else can use it, and singing while they do it.

choices.text: Walk the frontier to the wall, and watch the last fire

effects.log: Three seasons of walking. You arrive on the night of the fire. The soldiers sing the garrison's song until the granary roof falls in, and then walk south in a line with their spears reversed. An encampment ended. The Encampment plate lights. (-6 health)

choices.text: Send the snake to the capital to remind the court why the wall was built

ok.log: A minister dreams of a black snake reciting the old border wars to him, one by one, all night. The order is withdrawn. The garrison stays another century. There is nothing to write, and the snake is unbearable about it.

fail.log: The minister dreams of a snake and has the dream interpreter whipped. The garrison is disbanded anyway, without you to see it.

choices.text: Let the snake write it from what the river carries down: ash

effects.log: Ash in the river, from the north. The snake writes that the garrison was overrun and burnt. It was not overrun. The Encampment stars come up glowing wrong.

events.text: The Wall plate is bare: the mansion of writing, and of heaven's secret archive of books. A temple in the hills keeps a library of carved woodblocks, eighty years of a monk's life in every rack. A forest fire is coming over the ridge on a dry east wind, and the monks are carrying blocks out two at a time, and there are forty thousand.

choices.text: Lie in the temple pond and watch every rack burn, and remember the titles

effects.log: You watch from the pond until dawn and say the name of every sutra as its rack goes up. The monks, carrying, hear a voice under the water reciting their catalogue, and some of them weep. A library ended. The Wall plate lights, and it is very bright.

choices.text: Carry blocks out on your back through the smoke, as many as you can

effects.log: You carry four thousand blocks down to the river on your shell, stacked like firewood, and the snake bites embers off them on the way. A tenth of the library lives. The ending was changed, and there is nothing to write. The tortoise wanted to watch; the snake wanted to carry; this time the snake was right, and the tortoise knows it. (-14 health)

choices.text: Let the snake write it from what the monks say afterwards

effects.log: The monks say the fire was heaven's punishment for a lazy abbot. The snake writes it so. The Wall stars glow on your shell, wrong.

events.text: A winter night, and the snake reads your back through once and finds no bare plate and no wrong light. Dipper, Ox, Girl, Emptiness, Rooftop, Encampment, Wall: the whole northern sky is lying on the river ice, breathing. The snake, for the first time in seven hundred years, does not say anything clever. The tortoise, for the first time, says something first.

choices.text: Lie on the ice until dawn and let the villages see

effects.log: Three counties see the northern sky come down and lie on the river. Children are told what it means: somewhere, something is writing it all down, and getting it right.

choices.text: Ask the snake why it is quiet

effects.log: "Because it is all true," says the snake. "I have never had a whole sky of true before." The tortoise says that is the nicest thing the snake has ever said. The snake says it will deny it.

events.text: The Dipper plate aches in the frost, the crack across it glowing dull red. It is the old woman by the ford: the snake wrote that she died praying, and she did not. Her great-grandson is an old man now. He was in the room.

choices.text: Go back the long way, and find the truth

effects.log: You go back to the ford and lie under the window of the great-grandson, now ninety, and the snake asks. He laughs till he coughs. "Praying? She was telling a story about you, and she got your size wrong." The crack closes as you write it true. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let the snake lacquer over the crack with pine soot and river clay

effects.log: It looks perfect. In the frost it still aches, under the lacquer, like a tooth. The tortoise says nothing. The snake says that nobody will ever know. The tortoise says: one will.

choices.text: Not yet. The road is long and the frost is early

effects.log: You lie still and let it ache. It will still be there in spring, and the old people who remember will be a year older.

events.text: The Ox plate aches in the frost. The ferryman's last crossing: the snake wrote that he threw himself in after the rope. His granddaughter still keeps the ferry-house as an inn, and the old ferry hands drink there.

choices.text: Go back the long way, and find the truth

effects.log: A season at the inn's landing, listening. The old ferry hands remember it exactly: he cut the rope, watched it go, went home and slept for two days and woke up hungry. The crack closes as the truth goes over it. (-12 health)

choices.text: Go back the long way, and find the truth

effects.log: You go overland two villages and lie in the salt pans until a grandchild tells the story to a visiting cousin: the broken wedding, the salt merchant, fifty happy years and nine children. The crack closes. The snake is very quiet on the way home. (-12 health)

effects.log: You walk to the temple and lie under the bell all winter. The monks sing the garrison's song at the year's end, and the bell-ringer's great-grandchild tells it right: no enemy, an order, a fire, a song. The crack closes. (-12 health)

effects.log: You crawl up into the hills to the temple gate and read the stone, slowly, character by character, through the moss. A dry east wind, a careless charcoal burner, an abbot who died carrying blocks. The crack closes as the truth goes over it. (-12 health)

events.text: The word plates ache in the frost, the ones the snake delivered kinder than they were given. Somewhere, people are still living by a word that was never said: a son who thinks his father forgave him more than he did, a weaver who thinks the herdsman promised more than he promised. They are old now, or their children are.

choices.text: Go to every one of them, and say the word as it was given

effects.log: It takes twenty years and the hardest conversations of your life. Some weep. One throws a stone at the snake. One says, "I knew. I always knew it was too kind. Thank you." Every crack on the word plates closes. (-20 health)

choices.text: Let them keep the kinder words

effects.log: They are happy. The plates stay cracked. The snake says that a kind lie is a gift. The tortoise says a gift should not ache in the frost.

events.text: A messenger from the north, out of a far older country than this one: a king is dying in a land of high stone tombs, and a painter has worked a year in a granite chamber under a mound, painting the four walls. The east has its dragon, the west its tiger, the south its bird. On the north wall {npc} has stopped. "A tortoise and a snake wound round each other, their heads turned to face each other," {npc} tells the lamp. "Everyone paints it. Nobody has ever seen them do it. Mine look away from each other, like an old couple at a bad dinner."

choices.text: Go north, and lie in the lamplight of the tomb

effects.log: {npc} looks up from the lamp and sees you in the passage: black, the size of a threshing floor, stars on your plates, a snake round your shell. The brush falls. {He} picks it up with a hand that shakes, and begins.

choices.text: Send the snake into the painter's dream

effects.log: That night {npc} dreams of a black snake explaining at length how it would like to be painted, and from which side. In the morning {he} draws it before breakfast, and laughs, and sends to the river for the rest of you.

choices.text: A tomb is no place for the living. Stay on the river

effects.log: The north wall is finished from a pattern-book. The heads look away from each other. Nobody in the tomb will complain.

events.text: A lamp in a tomb mouth. You remember it: centuries ago, in a field of royal barrows, a painter on a scaffold saw you in the doorway at midnight and drew you on boards by one small flame. Now another king of the north is dying, and {npc}, that painter's heir by six generations, has walked to your river with the old boards wrapped in oiled cloth. "Every north wall my family has painted since was copied from these," {he} says. "They are not enough. My ancestor left a note: when the last king comes, fetch the tortoise itself."

choices.text: Follow {him} north

effects.log: Six generations of painters have waited for you. {npc} weeps a little at the sight of you, and then, being a painter, starts measuring.

choices.text: Ask what else the note says

effects.log: "It says: the heads must face," says {npc}, "and that the snake will argue." The snake argues that this is slander. You go north.

events.text: In the chamber {npc} has ground soot and cinnabar and ochre and mixed them with glue boiled from deer hide, and the plaster on the north wall is wet. "Now," {he} says. "Turn your heads to each other, and hold it." And you cannot hold it. The heads have faced each other before, for a breath, for a crowd or a painter, and turned away again. In all those centuries the tortoise has always looked ahead and the snake has always looked out, over the shell, for danger. The lamp burns down. The plaster is drying.

choices.text: Let the snake come round the shell to the front, slowly

effects.log: It takes the snake an hour to come round, coil by coil, and then it is there, face to face with the tortoise, closer than it has ever been, and neither of them knows what to say. {npc} paints like a person on fire. It is finished before the plaster dries.

choices.text: Turn both heads at once, together

effects.log: You do it together, the slow head and the quick one, and meet in the middle, and for one breath you see yourself from the outside: one creature, wound round itself, looking at itself. {npc} paints it in one stroke without lifting the brush.

choices.text: Tell {him} to paint you as you are: looking away

effects.log: {npc} paints you looking away, honestly, and it is the best tortoise anyone ever painted and the saddest. You leave before the lamp goes out.

events.text: The king of the north is buried. The stone door is sliding shut, and in the last of the torchlight four guardians stand on four walls round a sleeper who was afraid of the dark. The north wall is yours: a tortoise and a snake, wound round each other, heads turned face to face, wet and black and alive. You could step into it. The painting would hold you; it was made to. One sleeper, thirteen hundred years, and the colour going grain by grain.

choices.text: Leave a scute of your shell in the plaster, and go

effects.log: You press one small plate from the edge of your shell into the wet wall, under the two heads. It takes the colour and becomes part of the painting. The door closes. Once every few hundred years you feel that dark like an itch at the edge of the shell.

choices.text: Go, and let the painting be a painting

effects.log: The door closes on a good painting. Paintings fade. The snake says that kings are not afraid of anything once they are dead. The tortoise is not so sure, and looks back.

choices.text: Step into the north wall

effects.log: You step into the soot and the cinnabar, both heads still turned to each other, and the door closes, and it is dark, and for the first time in your life neither head is looking out for danger. Thirteen centuries. The king goes to dust. The black flakes off the granite grain by grain, until only the two heads are left, still facing. One day a lamp comes in, and someone gasps, and you are still there.

events.text: Long after, an itch at the edge of the shell: grave-robbers in the tomb of the north. They have dug through the mound and are prying at the stone door with iron bars. Inside, the four guardians are only paint, except where one small plate of real shell is set into the plaster of the north wall.

choices.text: Turn the painted heads to look at them

effects.log: They get the door open, lift the lamp, and on the north wall a tortoise and a snake that were facing each other turn, slowly, and face them. The robbers are found a week later in the next county, still running.

choices.text: Let the earth fall back over the door

effects.log: A small landslide, very precise. The door is buried again. The robbers dig somewhere else, and the king sleeps on.

events.text: Something has been happening to the snake all winter. It is heavier, longer, and it no longer lies along the rim of the shell looking out. One morning on the ice it comes round, the whole length of it, coil over coil, until it is in front of you, and lifts its head, and looks the tortoise in the eye. It has done it before, for a breath, and always turned away. This time it stays. Neither of you blinks. It is like looking at yourself in black water and finding someone else there.

choices.text: Hold its gaze until the sun is up

effects.log: The sun comes up over the frozen sea. Neither of you looks away. Somewhere in the middle of the morning you stop being able to tell which of you is looking and which is being looked at. That, the old books say, is the Black Warrior.

choices.text: Say the first thing, after nine hundred years

effects.log: The tortoise says: "Oh. It is you." The snake says: "Who did you think it was?" Then both of you laugh, and the ice cracks for a mile in each direction.

choices.text: Look away first, out of habit

effects.log: The tortoise looks away first. The snake stays where it is, in front, and waits, as long as it takes, which turns out to be three years. Then the tortoise looks back.

events.text: A ferry child, eight years old, has fallen asleep on your back thinking you are a rock in the shallows, and wakes, and sees the snake looking at {him}, and does not scream. "Can the other one talk too?" {npc} asks. In nine hundred years, every word you ever said to a human was the snake's. The tortoise has never once spoken.

choices.text: Let the tortoise answer, for itself, for the first time

mem.note: heard the old head speak first

effects.log: It takes a long time. The voice, when it comes, is slow and low and has river-silt in it. "Yes," says the tortoise. "But not often." {npc} nods, satisfied, and goes back to sleep on your back, and the snake is so astonished it does not speak for a week.

choices.text: Let the snake answer, as it always has

effects.log: "It can," says the snake. "It does not need to. It has me." {npc} looks at the tortoise for a long time. "It looks like it wants to," {he} says. The tortoise does not deny it.

events.text: A war-band of hunters from over the mountains, forty of them, with iron chain and a diviner's brazier on a sled, has cornered you on the ice of a bay. They have heard about the shell: shut it, and you are a stone; leave the snake out, and they will take its head. Their leader is laughing. They have never seen what you are now.

choices.text: Put forth your head: shut the shell, then both heads strike at once

effects.log: The shell closes and they come forward with the chain, and then both heads come out at once, the slow one and the quick one, from two sides, and nobody can watch two places. The chain goes into the sea. The leader goes into the sea after it. The other thirty-nine walk home over the ice to tell everyone.

choices.text: The snake goes out alone, as it always has

ok.log: The snake does it alone, as it always has, and it is enough, just. Forty hunters run. Afterwards the tortoise says, quietly, that it could have helped. The snake says it knows.

fail.log: Forty men and iron chain are too much for one head. The snake comes back bleeding into the shell, and you lie shut on the ice for nine days until they give up.
fail.deathCause: a war-band's iron chain on the ice of a northern bay

choices.text: Draw in, and let them break their spears on the shell

effects.log: Nine days of spears and fire on the shell. They break everything they brought. On the tenth day they go home, and you open, and the snake says that was the most boring war in history. (-8 health)

events.text: A northern army camps on your river under its directional flags, and on the black one, the banner of the north, an embroiderer has stitched you: a tortoise and a snake, wound together, the heads facing. The soldiers call it the Black Warrior. The general who rides under it is young, frightened, and marching to a war the snake says will end badly. The tortoise says it is not your war.

choices.text: Rise out of the river under the banner, once, and let them see

effects.log: Ten thousand men see the black banner come alive out of the river and look at them, both heads at once. The general dismounts and bows. The army does not march that year. Whether that was right, the snake says, will take a century to know.

choices.text: Stay under the ice. Banners are for humans

effects.log: They march. The black banner comes home torn the next spring, carried by half as many men. The tortoise writes nothing; it was not an ending yours to see. It aches anyway.

choices.text: Let the snake whisper to the general what the omen says

effects.log: The general listens, and goes anyway, and wins, against every omen. The snake is furious for a decade. The tortoise is quietly pleased: the snake is not always right, and it is good to know.

events.text: The heads have argued for centuries about which way is forward. Now, face to face, they have found a new argument: which of them is the face of the Black Warrior. The snake says it is obviously the snake; it is the one on the banners. The tortoise says nothing, which is its argument.

choices.text: Settle it: neither. The face is the space between

effects.log: The snake considers this for a whole winter and decides it is annoyingly good. The tortoise says it was the snake's idea. The snake says it was not. They are, at least, arguing about something new.

choices.text: Let the snake win this one

effects.log: The snake wins, and is so suspicious of winning that it gives the point back by spring.

choices.text: Let the tortoise win this one, for once

effects.log: The tortoise wins. It does not know what to do with winning. It puts it away somewhere safe and never mentions it again.

events.text: A prince of the southern kingdom comes up your river with stone carvers and a cord knotted every hand-span. {npc} is a calligrapher, the second son of a king who died this spring. "My father was a prisoner in the north once, as a young envoy," {he} says to the water. "My father escaped by a story about a turtle and a rabbit, and made me swear that at the end, the finest turtle in the land would carry the royal name. The carvers say that is you."

choices.text: Let them measure you

effects.log: They measure you with the knotted cord for three days, nose to tail and plate by plate, and argue about the hexagons. {npc} sits on the bank and grinds ink and watches you the whole time, as if trying to learn something.

choices.text: Ask what the stele will say

effects.log: "What my father did," says {npc}. "Most of it. Not the turtle and the rabbit; that is undignified." The snake says the turtle and the rabbit is the only part anyone will remember. {npc} laughs for the first time since the funeral.

choices.text: Sink to the bottom and wait for them to leave

effects.log: They wait a week, then carve a turtle from a pattern-book. It is a good turtle, a little stiff.

events.text: A prince of the southern kingdom at your river with stone carvers and a knotted cord, and you know the face: it is the face of the young envoy in the prison well, long ago, the night a courtier told the prisoner a story of a turtle and a rabbit, and the well helped the prisoner understand it. That envoy founded a line of kings. "Every king of my house has asked for the turtle of the well to carry the royal stele," says {npc}. "None of them found it. My father died this spring. I found it."

choices.text: "It was the snake, in the well"

effects.log: {npc} stares at the snake. The snake bows. "The founder always wrote that the well understood the story before {he} did," says {npc} slowly. "We thought it was the fever."

choices.text: Let them measure you, in silence

effects.log: You lie still for the knotted cord, and think about a prisoner in a well who did not know a crown was coming, and you were there, and nobody wrote it down.

events.text: The great slab for the stele is cut, and {npc} is writing the text in brush on paper before it goes onto the stone: the king's wars, the king's laws, the king's piety. The snake has read it over {his} shoulder and has opinions. "Put in the well," it says. "Put in the rabbit. Nobody will remember the laws."

choices.text: Let the snake bargain for one line about the turtle and the rabbit

ok.log: {npc} argues for a night and gives in at dawn. One line, small, at the very bottom: freed by a turtle's story. The snake is happier than it has been in a century.

fail.log: "Undignified," says {npc}, firmly. The snake sulks for a decade. The laws go onto the stone.

choices.text: Let the tortoise ask {him} to write only what is true

effects.log: {npc} reads it over again with that in mind and crosses out three victories. "Those were losses," {he} admits. "Everybody knows." The stele will be shorter and truer, and the tortoise approves of both.

events.text: The tomb field of the southern kings, in autumn. The stele is carved and stands on rollers. Before it, the stone base waits to be cut: a turtle, the carvers say, to carry the king's name for ever. {npc} looks at you and does not ask. {He} has been carefully not asking for a year. Your plates are the hexagons the carvers have been drawing.

choices.text: Lie in the field for the carvers instead, and let them cut a stone you

effects.log: For a year you lie in the tomb field as a model while they cut the base: head lifted, striding, cheerful, every hexagon true. When it is finished {npc} brings you to see it. The snake says the stone one looks smug. The tortoise says the stone one looks happy. They are both right.

choices.text: Go home. Let the stone carry the name

effects.log: The base is cut from a pattern-book. {npc} walks with you as far as the river and says that {his} father would have laughed. You believe it.

choices.text: Lie down under it of your own will, head lifted, and become stone

effects.log: You walk up into the tomb field and lie down where the base should be, and lift your head high, and stride, the way you have always walked when you were pleased to be going somewhere. The stele comes down onto your back. The stone climbs up through you, cool and slow and not unpleasant. Centuries later the stele itself is lost. You are not. You are still striding, head up, cheerful, in a field of grass.

events.text: The tomb field of the southern kings, a thousand years after the stele went up. The slab was lost to a soldiers' hearth long ago; now an earthquake has split the stone turtle too, from the neck to the tail. The last heirs of the old line have come with new stone cut from the old rubbings, to raise the stele again, and they are standing round the broken turtle not knowing what to do. You promised the stone you would come back when the stele fell.

choices.text: Mend the stone turtle instead, and let them raise it on that

effects.log: You lie against the broken stone for a season, and the cold of you seeps into the crack and draws it shut, the way frost closes a road. The heirs raise the new slab on the mended turtle. The promise is kept another way, and the stone, you think, does not mind. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell the heirs, through the snake, to let the field rest

effects.log: The snake tells them that some things are finished when they fall. They listen, and leave the broken turtle in the grass. The tortoise goes on feeling that it broke a promise, very quietly, for a hundred years.

choices.text: Keep the promise: lie down where the stone turtle lay, and take the stele

effects.log: You walk into the tomb field at dawn, past the heirs, who fall back, and lie down where the broken turtle lay, and lift your head high, and stride, as the stone one did, cheerful. They lower the new slab onto your back with ropes and prayers. The stone climbs up through you, cool and slow and not unpleasant. Centuries later this stele too is lost. You are not. You are still striding, head up, in a field of grass.

events.text: The stele you once lay beside is gone, carried off in a war; only the stone turtle you sat for remains in the tomb field, head lifted, striding. Children climb on it. A scholar measures it and writes that it is the finest stone turtle in the land, and that nobody knows who the carvers copied.

choices.text: Lie beside it in the grass one afternoon

effects.log: Two black shells in a tomb field, one stone and one not. A child climbs from one to the other without noticing the difference, until the second one breathes.

choices.text: Let the snake read the scholar's notes over his shoulder

effects.log: Nobody knows who the carvers copied, the scholar writes. The snake hisses a correction into his dream. He wakes, crosses out the line, and writes instead: perhaps a real one.

events.text: A dark age in the south: no king, three famines, war-bands on every road. Far down the rivers, so faint you feel it in your plates before you hear it, a crowd is singing on a hill. You know the song. Every turtle knows it. "Turtle, turtle, put forth your head; if you do not, we will roast you and eat you." They are digging up the earth of the summit and throwing it in the air, the way their ancestors did, nine chiefs and a whole valley, singing at the sky for a king.

choices.text: Go south, toward the song

effects.log: A whole season down the rivers and overland, with the song getting louder every night. The snake says nobody has ever answered it twice. The tortoise says nobody has ever tried. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let the snake put forth its head, here, a thousand miles away

effects.log: The snake lifts its head out of the river and says, very loudly, "Here." Nothing happens. A thousand miles away the singing goes on. The snake is offended. The tortoise is already turning south.

choices.text: Stay. The song is for kings, not turtles

effects.log: The song goes on all autumn, fainter and fainter. The tortoise lies still and listens to every verse. The snake pretends not to.

events.text: The song again, after so long. Centuries ago nine chiefs sang it at you on a turtle-headed hill, digging the earth all round you, and you answered after a fashion, and then a golden box came down on a purple rope and they forgot about you entirely. Now their descendants are on the same hill, in a dark age, singing it at the sky. The snake says, quietly, that this time it would like the tortoise to come too.

choices.text: Go south, together

effects.log: The snake talks the whole way, about the first time, the box, the eggs, the chief who wept. The tortoise listens to every word, which is new.

choices.text: Go south, and let the snake lead

effects.log: The snake leads, fast and sure, and the tortoise follows a long way behind, arriving a week late and entirely calm.

events.text: The hill like a turtle's head, at dusk. Nine chiefs and a whole valley in hemp, singing, scattering the earth of the summit. A dolmen on the top, older than any of them. They see you come up out of the stream at the foot of the hill, black, plated with stars, and the song stops dead in the middle of a word. "Turtle, turtle," says one old chief, into the silence, shaking. "Put forth your head."

choices.text: Let only the snake put forth its head

effects.log: The snake rises out of the shell and looks at the nine chiefs. The nine chiefs look at each other. "Does that count?" asks one. Nobody knows. They argue all night, and by morning one of them has made himself king by sheer stubbornness, and the snake says that is close enough.

choices.text: Let only the tortoise put forth its head

effects.log: The tortoise puts out its old slow head, and the chiefs wait for something more, and it does not come, and slowly they understand that this is a turtle that will wait longer than they will. They go home and choose a king among themselves, carefully, as if someone patient were watching. Someone is.

choices.text: Go back into the stream. They need a king, not a turtle

effects.log: You sink back into the water. The singing starts again, slower, and at dawn they stop singing and start talking. It takes them a year to choose. It is a better choice for the year.

choices.text: Put forth your head: both of them, together

effects.log: You draw both heads in, and then you put them forth, together, the slow one and the quick one, and the valley gasps. And you keep putting forth: your shell spreads over the summit, your heads become two spurs of the ridge, the dolmen sits on your back like a crown. You are the hill. At midnight a light comes down out of the sky onto you, and a box on a purple rope, and in the morning there is a child on the dolmen who will be a king, and the valley never sings at the sky again. They sing at you.

events.text: The hill like a turtle's head, a hundred years after the singing. The king they chose is dead, and his son is king, and on the first night of the third month the whole valley still climbs the hill and digs up a handful of earth and throws it in the air, and sings. Nobody remembers why. Somebody always says they once saw a turtle.

choices.text: Lie in the stream at the foot of the hill all night

effects.log: They sing until midnight. A child at the back of the crowd sees a black shell in the stream, and does not tell anybody, and grows up to be the one who always says it.

choices.text: Let the snake hum along, very quietly

effects.log: The snake hums the old tune under the water. The tortoise, to everyone's surprise, hums too, flat. The valley hears the hill humming and decides it is a good year, and it is.

events.text: Dusk, and the far bank of your river is full of people: a kingdom is falling somewhere behind them, and they have walked from it for nine days. Old men with ancestral tablets on their backs, a weaver bent under a loom, a child carrying a goose. Their leader, {npc}, a young archer with a broken bow, stands at the water's edge and looks at the flood. There is no ferry. The horsemen are a day behind. "My grandmother said the river would help," {he} says, to nobody. "Grandmother said the river owed us."

choices.text: Come up out of the water where {he} can see you

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time. Then {he} kneels in the mud, and the whole column kneels behind, and the child with the goose asks very loudly if that is the river. The snake says yes.

choices.text: Carry a few across on your back through the night

effects.log: Forty at a time, all night, in the flood. By dawn you have carried four hundred, and there are four thousand. {npc} counts them over on the far bank, and comes back to the water, and waits. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let the snake tell them to go upstream to the ford

effects.log: They go upstream in the dark. Some of them make the ford. You do not see the rest. The tortoise says nothing about it, for a very long time.

events.text: Dusk on your river, and a column of refugees on the far bank with horsemen a day behind them. Their leader, {npc}, an archer with a broken bow, strikes the water with the bow and names a father in the sky and a grandfather in the river, the way a young archer did long ago, when you were one turtle among a thousand that rose. This one is the grandchild of that archer's grandchild, and this time the fish are fewer, and the turtles are old.

choices.text: Rise first, so the others follow

effects.log: You come up under the bow, and then the fish and the turtles come up behind you, fewer than before, older, and they look at you as if you were the one they had been waiting for. Perhaps you are.

choices.text: Tell {him}, through the snake, that it worked once because it was needed once

effects.log: {npc} listens. "It is needed now," {he} says. The snake cannot think of an answer to that, and neither can the tortoise.

events.text: Dawn. Every fish and turtle in your river has answered, and they have risen, back to back, a bridge across the flood, and the column is crossing on it: tablets, looms, the goose. {npc} is last, walking backwards, bow up. The horsemen come down to the near bank with torches. When {npc} steps off, the fish and the turtles will have to sink, and the river will close. Unless one of them stays.

choices.text: Sink with the others when the last one is over

effects.log: The last child steps off with the goose. The bridge goes down under the horsemen's noses, all at once. On the far bank {npc} raises the broken bow to the river, and you raise both heads, and the column walks on toward a country nobody has named yet.

choices.text: Sink only when the first horsemen are on the bridge

effects.log: They ride out onto the backs of the fish, and the snake says now, and the bridge goes down. The river takes forty horsemen. The rest turn back. The refugees on the far bank are saved, and they saw it, and they are afraid of the river for ever after. The tortoise says nothing for a hundred years.

choices.text: Stay. Become the causeway

effects.log: The others sink, as they must, and you do not. You set your feet in the riverbed and let the stone come up through you, plate by plate, until you are a long black causeway from bank to bank with a snake of black stone along its rim. The horsemen look at it and turn back: nobody crosses a river on a god. On the far side, by the end of that year, there is a town, and in a lifetime a kingdom, and its children are taught to bow to the causeway before they cross.

events.text: On the far bank of your river there is a kingdom now, small and stubborn, founded by people who crossed on the backs of fish. Every spring their king comes down to the water with a black ox and a bowl of rice, and pours the rice into the river, and says the river's name, which they have made up, and which is almost right.

choices.text: Rise once, and let the king see you

effects.log: The king, a grandchild of the archer, drops the bowl. The court will talk of nothing else for a year. The rice is excellent.

choices.text: Stay under, and eat the rice

effects.log: Good rice, every spring, for three hundred years. The snake says it is the only tax in history it has ever approved of.

events.text: A war on the southern coast: ships from over the sea, hundreds, and a fleet that has burnt every harbour from here to the capital. On the shore of your estuary at night, {npc}, an admiral of the south, sits on a rock with a lamp and a sheaf of paper and draws turtles. {He} has drawn every turtle in the province. {He} has not seen you yet. "A covered ship," {he} says to the lamp. "A back nobody can board. A head that frightens them before the cannon do."
events.arc: The Turtle Head at the Bow

choices.text: Come up out of the estuary in front of the lamp

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time. Then {he} turns to a clean sheet and starts again, and draws all night. In the morning there are nine sheets, and on the ninth the ship has your shape.

choices.text: Let the snake show {him} where to put the spikes

effects.log: The snake lies along the curve of your shell and taps, with its nose, every place a boarding man would put a foot. {npc} draws an iron spike at each one, faster and faster, laughing under {his} breath.

choices.text: Sink. A shell is for keeping, not for war

effects.log: {npc} draws on without you. The ship is built anyway, from the province's turtles. It is a good ship, a little slow to turn.

events.text: The admiral who once sat on a rock drawing turtles by lamplight is long dead, and the covered ship rotted in its harbour long ago. Now the raiders are back, more of them, and {npc}, an admiral of the same coast, has found the old shipwrights' copies in a temple chest and come to your estuary with them under {his} arm. "They say a turtle kept this coast once," {he} says. "They say it watched from the water. I am building the ship again."
events.arc: The Turtle Head at the Bow

choices.text: Let {him} build it, and lie in the shipyard as a model

effects.log: A whole winter in the shipyard mud while the carpenters measure you, and the blacksmiths beat out iron spikes, and the snake corrects them all.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the war is for

effects.log: "For the coast," says {npc}. "For the fishing villages. Nothing else; there is nothing else here." It is the right answer. You stay.

events.text: The ship is launched: a long covered back of planks and iron spikes, oars in rows, and at the bow a carved turtle's head with a throat of iron, where they will burn sulphur and saltpetre so that it breathes smoke like sea fog. The crew is afraid of it. {npc} asks one thing of you: swim beneath it in its first battle, so that it is not alone.
events.arc: The Turtle Head at the Bow

choices.text: Swim beneath it

ok.log: Thirteen enemy ships in a narrow strait. The covered ship goes into the middle of them breathing smoke, and nobody can board it, and under it, unseen, something holds it steady in every wave. Thirteen ships burn. The crew stops being afraid of the head.

fail.log: A cannon ball goes into the water beside the hull and finds your shell. The ship wins. You limp home to the estuary with a plate chipped by iron, not by a lie, which the snake says is at least honest. (-18 health)

choices.text: Watch from the estuary, as a witness

effects.log: You watch the first battle from the mouth of the estuary. The ship wins without you. The tortoise is proud of it, the way you are proud of a drawing of yourself that came out better than you.

events.text: The last great battle of the war, in a strait where the tide runs like a river. Three hundred ships against a dozen. {npc} stands on the deck of the covered ship, and the turtle head at the bow is cold, because the sulphur ran out at dawn, and the crew know it. "It needs a guardian," {npc} says, not looking at the water. "It was always meant to have one."
events.arc: The Turtle Head at the Bow

choices.text: Guard the strait from beneath through one battle, and come home

effects.log: All day under the hull in the tide-race, holding it steady while the cannons go, turning it when the oarsmen cannot. At sunset the strait is clear. {npc} pours a jar of rice liquor into the estuary that night and does not say what it is for. (-15 health)

choices.text: Refuse. You are a witness, not a warship

effects.log: You watch the last battle from the cliffs. The ship wins anyway, by a hair, with a cold head. {npc} never asks again, and never blames you, and that is harder than blame.

choices.text: Go into the bow

effects.log: You go up into the carved head at the bow the way water goes into a jar, and the iron throat fills with a smoke that is not sulphur at all, but the cold black breath of the north. The covered ship goes into three hundred, and nobody can board it, and nobody can see through its smoke, and at sunset the strait is clear. You guard that coast through that war and the next, in the head at the bow. Centuries later a scholar writes that it was a dragon's head. It was not.

events.text: A scholar in a fine hat stands on the shore of your estuary, long after the war, with a book in which {npc} has written that the covered ship of the old admiral bore a dragon's head at its bow. {npc} is reading it aloud to students. The snake has gone very still.
events.arc: The Turtle Head at the Bow

choices.text: Rise, and put forth your head next to the drawing

effects.log: The students see a black head rise out of the estuary, look at the drawing in the book, and look at {npc}. {npc} looks at the head and at the drawing for a long time and then, carefully, crosses out one word.

choices.text: Let it go. A dragon is a better story

effects.log: The tortoise lets it go. The snake does not, quite: that night every student dreams of a turtle with a cold black breath. None of them ever writes dragon again.

events.text: The snake reads it in the eddies under the ford: a youth in the village, {npc}, the only child of a charcoal-burner, will die at nineteen, and is eighteen now. A wandering monk has seen it too, and sent {him} up the mountain with a jar of rice liquor and a strip of dried venison, to a mulberry tree where two old men play baduk, with orders to serve them in silence and say nothing until they speak. {npc} has no idea why. You do.

choices.text: Follow {npc} up the mountain

effects.log: You go up behind {npc} through the pines, slowly, and arrive a day later. {He} is kneeling by the rock, pouring, silent. The two old men have not looked up. One of them, without looking, says: "You are late."

choices.text: Let the snake go ahead and speak first

effects.log: The snake is up the mountain first. When {npc} arrives, the snake is coiled on the rock between the two old men, and the stern one is looking at it with great distaste.

choices.text: Let the ending come. It is the Dipper's, not yours

effects.log: You lie under the ford all year. {npc} comes down from the mountain alive, at nineteen, and at twenty, and the snake says somebody must have spoken up. It sounds jealous.

events.text: A youth at the ford with a jar and a strip of dried venison, being sent up the mountain to two old men at baduk because of a death at nineteen. You have seen this before, centuries ago. Then you noticed, at the end, how one of the old men sat like a tortoise and the other coiled like a snake. The snake has not forgotten. "Go," it says. "I want to see their faces this time." The youth is called {npc}.

choices.text: Follow {npc} up the mountain

effects.log: The mulberry, the flat rock, the board. The two old men are older than you remember. The fair one looks up at you and smiles as if at family. The stern one does not look up at all.

choices.text: Send the snake on ahead with a message for the stern one

effects.log: The message is: "We remember." The stern old man reads it off the snake's face and, for the first time in a thousand years, very nearly smiles.

events.text: The game ends. The two old men notice the jar, and the venison, and drink and eat, and only then notice {npc}. The fair one wants to help. The stern one, the keeper of the register of death, says it is written and that is that. Then they both turn, as one, and look at you. "Well?" says the fair one. "You are the witness," says the stern one. "Witnesses do not argue," says the fair one. "This one does," says the stern one, looking at the snake.

choices.text: Let the snake argue, and the tortoise agree

effects.log: The snake argues for an hour, brilliantly. The tortoise says one word at the end: "Yes." The stern old man sighs, opens the register, and turns a nineteen into a ninety-nine with one stroke. {npc} goes down the mountain with eighty more years and no idea what happened.

choices.text: Say nothing. A witness writes; it does not plead

effects.log: You say nothing. The two old men argue between themselves for a long time, as they always do, and in the end they make it up, and the fair one changes the number anyway. The stern one looks at you afterwards, approving, and you realise you have just been tested.

choices.text: Ask who they really are

effects.log: "The Dipper of the south, who writes the living in," says the fair one. "The Dipper of the north, who writes them out," says the stern one. "And before that?" asks the snake. They look at each other. "Before that," they say together, "we were very much like you." Then they change the nineteen to ninety-nine and go back to their game.

events.text: Years later, the mulberry on the mountain. The two old men are waiting for you, and for once they are not playing. The board is set up between two empty places. "We are tired," says the fair one. "We have been doing this since the first child was born," says the stern one. "A tortoise and a snake," they say together, "would do it very well. One kind, one stern. One writes them in; one writes them out." They put down their stones.

choices.text: Play one game with them first, and decline

effects.log: One game, all night. The snake plays the stern one and loses. The tortoise plays the kind one and wins by half a point. At dawn they pack up the board, a little disappointed, and the stern one says: "We will ask again in a thousand years." The charcoal-burner's family, down in the valley, have children who live past nineteen for ever after.

choices.text: Tell them the north has another seat waiting

effects.log: They nod, as if they knew. "The Northern Palace," says the fair one. "Our old house," says the stern one. "Give it our regards." They go back to their game, and you go back down the mountain, the snake very quiet.

choices.text: Take the board

effects.log: You sit down at the rock under the mulberry, and the snake takes the stern place, and the tortoise takes the kind one, though everyone expected it the other way round. The register of lives is open between you. Every few generations a youth who should die at nineteen climbs the mountain with a jar and a strip of venison, and the snake argues, and the tortoise agrees, and nineteen becomes ninety-nine. The two old men walk off down the mountain together, arguing, and are never seen again.

events.text: Byeolju comes up the river, the Dragon King's turtle official in the black gauze hat, so old now that the hat is green with weed. It has a kelp scroll and a very formal manner. "His Majesty," says Byeolju, "is minded to retire his oldest minister, which is me. His Majesty has asked who in the four seas should have my chair. I said: the one in the north with two heads. His Majesty said: both of them? I said: they come as a pair."

choices.text: Go down to the palace and look at the chair

effects.log: Byeolju swims ahead of you down into the blue, slowly, its hat bobbing, telling you which minister to avoid at dinner and which fish never pays its debts. The snake listens to all of it with deep professional interest.

choices.text: Ask Byeolju why it is retiring

effects.log: "Because I went ashore once for a rabbit's liver," says Byeolju, "and came back without it, and have been apologising for eleven hundred years. I should like to stop." It says it without bitterness. Then it asks if you would like to see the chair.

choices.text: Decline. The rivers need their tortoise

effects.log: Byeolju bows, entirely unsurprised, and swims back down to the sea. "His Majesty always asks again," it says over its shoulder.

events.text: A season in the coral halls. The chair of the oldest minister is mother-of-pearl, worn smooth, beside a round window that looks out into the dark of the deep. From it you can see every river mouth in the four seas and every word carried up them. The Dragon King, old and kind and slightly deaf, asks your opinion on a quarrel between two river gods, and asks both heads, separately, and listens to both.

choices.text: Give him the tortoise's answer: wait a hundred years

effects.log: The Dragon King laughs until the coral shakes. "Byeolju said you would say that." The two river gods wait a hundred years and by then have forgotten what they were quarrelling about. It is the best ruling of the century.

choices.text: Give him the snake's answer: join the rivers

effects.log: The snake proposes joining the two rivers above the disputed reach, and the Dragon King, delighted, decrees it. A new river is born. Its fish are very confused for a decade.

choices.text: Give him both answers, side by side, and let him choose

effects.log: The Dragon King reads both on a kelp scroll, slowly, and chooses neither, and makes a third from the two, and says it is the first time in a thousand years anyone has given him a choice instead of an answer.

events.text: The Dragon King sends for you to the throne hall. Byeolju stands at the side in its weedy hat, holding a new one: the hat of the oldest minister, black gauze, freshly starched, with two long ribbons, one for each head. "The oldest chair in the four seas," says the Dragon King. "Carry my words to the rivers for ever. Or go back to them, and carry your own."

choices.text: Decline, and ask that Byeolju be allowed to rest anyway

effects.log: The Dragon King grants it. Byeolju retires to a quiet grotto with a view of the kelp, and writes you a letter every hundred years, entirely about the rabbit.

choices.text: Ask for a century to think

effects.log: "A century," says the Dragon King, "is how long a tortoise blinks. Granted." Byeolju puts the new hat away in a lacquer box, carefully, for later.

choices.text: Take the hat and the chair

effects.log: Byeolju puts the hat on your head itself, and has to stand on a clam to reach. You take the chair by the round window, and the snake takes the correspondence, and the tortoise takes the long view. For ever after, when a well god or a river spirit or a magistrate dreams of a black tortoise in a gauze hat bringing word from the deep, it is you, unhurried, carrying the sea up the rivers one word at a time. It is the quietest good ending there is.

events.text: Three warm winters in a row, and the river by the capital has not frozen thick enough to cut. The royal ice house stands empty; in summer there will be no ice for the ancestral rites, the sick, the dead. The court performs the old rite to the north god who governs cold: a black ox, black millet, a peach-wood bow and thorn arrows hung in the dark of the ice chamber. They wait. The god of the rite has not answered in a hundred years. Your shell feels it like a hand laid on it.

choices.text: Answer the rite: freeze the river in one night

effects.log: You lie down in the river under the palace walls and breathe out, slowly, all night. By dawn the ice is four fingers thick, the thickness the old rule asks for, and the ice cutters are out with their saws, weeping with cold and relief.

choices.text: Let the snake ask who will cut the ice

effects.log: Conscripts from the riverside villages, the snake finds, unpaid, in the worst month of the year, and some of them die of it every winter. You freeze the river anyway, but only after a minister dreams of black water and pays the cutters for the first time in the ice house's history.

choices.text: Let the warm winters be. Cold is not owed to kings

effects.log: The ice house stays empty. In summer the rites are made without ice, and the dead are buried quickly, and the court blames a minister. Nobody blames you. Nobody knows to.

events.text: Midsummer, and the ice you made is in use: a sick prince with a fever has ice on his forehead; the queen dowager, dead nine days, lies on blocks of it in the hall while the mourning goes on; the ancestral shrine has its offerings cooled. And the ice is going fast. It was a hot spring. The ice-house keeper, an old man, counts the blocks every morning and prays to a god he has never seen.

choices.text: Lie in the river below the ice house all summer, cold

effects.log: The ice lasts to the first frost, exactly. The keeper never understands it. Every morning he counts and there is a block more than there should be. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let the snake visit the keeper's dream with the old rule

effects.log: Straw packed between the blocks, the door opened only before dawn, the drain kept clear. The keeper wakes and does all of it. The ice lasts. The snake is smug all summer.

events.text: The warm winters will not stop. The snake has read it in the stars on your back: a hundred years of them, maybe more, and the ice house of the capital empty in every one. Without ice there are no summer rites, no relief for the fevers, no cool for the dead. You could freeze the river every winter, as you have. Or you could go into the ice house itself, under the floor, and be the cold.

choices.text: Freeze the river every winter, for as long as it takes

effects.log: A hundred winters. Every one, you come down to the capital and lie under the walls and breathe the river solid. You are very tired by the end of it, and so is the snake, and the ice house is never empty. (-10 health)

choices.text: Teach the ice cutters to dig a deeper house in a colder valley

effects.log: The snake shows them a valley where the frost lies late, and the tortoise shows them how deep the cold goes in the ground. They build a second ice house there, of stone, half underground, with a drain and a straw roof, and it works without you. That was the point.

choices.text: Lie down under the royal ice house and keep the cold

effects.log: You go down through the floor of the ice house into the earth beneath and lie there, and breathe out, and do not breathe in again. From then on the ice house never fails, in any summer, however hot. The king has ice. The sick have ice. The dead are kept cool for their funerals. The keepers come and go, generation after generation, and every one of them finds the floor of the chamber cold as a river in the twelfth month, and nobody knows why.

events.text: On the wall of the west ice house there is still a board, black with age, that the officials think is a charm. It is the promise you made the keeper's family: the ice will not fail while you live. Now the winters are failing for good. The snake has read it in the stars on your back: a century of warm ones, maybe more. The keeper's great-great-grandchild stands in the drainage channel at night, holding a lamp, and does not say anything. The way under the floor is the way you learned by heart, every turn of it.

choices.text: Freeze the river every winter instead, for as long as it takes

effects.log: A hundred winters. Every one, you come down to the capital and lie under the walls and breathe the river solid. The promise holds. You are very tired by the end of it, and so is the snake. (-10 health)

choices.text: Show the keeper a colder valley for a second ice house

effects.log: The snake shows the keeper a valley where the frost lies late, and the tortoise shows how deep the cold goes in the ground. A second ice house goes up there, half underground, with a drain and a straw roof, and it works without you. The promise is kept by teaching, which the tortoise says is the best way to keep one.

choices.text: Go up the channel, lie down under the ice house, and keep the cold

effects.log: You go up the drainage channel in the dark, every turn of it as you remembered, and lie down under the stone floor of the ice house, and breathe out, and do not breathe in again. From then on the ice house never fails, in any summer, however hot. The king has ice. The sick have ice. The dead are kept cool for their funerals. The family of the keepers hangs a new board beside the old one, and the officials think it is another charm. Nobody else knows why.

events.text: The snake has unwound three turns from your shell and lies beside you on the riverbed now, not round you. It does not explain. It looks upstream a great deal, toward the mountains, where the old stories say there is a pool under a waterfall where a serpent can wait a thousand years and rise a dragon. The tortoise looks the other way, at a round rock on the bank, and thinks how restful it would be to be a rock.

choices.text: Let the heads talk, all winter, about anything at all

effects.log: It is hard at first. Then the snake tells a story the tortoise has heard a hundred times, and the tortoise laughs at the right place for the first time in a century, and the snake winds one turn back round the shell without seeming to notice.

choices.text: Ask the snake, plainly, if it wants to go

effects.log: "I do not know," says the snake, which is the most honest thing it has said in years. "Do you want me to?" "No," says the tortoise. They lie side by side and think about that.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let it look upstream

effects.log: It looks upstream all winter. You look at the rock. In spring neither of you has moved, and something between you has.

events.text: The snake goes upstream in the night, unwinding the last coils one by one, and you follow it, because you are still joined at the root and cannot do otherwise. At dawn you are at the pool under the waterfall, dark and still, and in the shallows at its edge the snake has stretched itself out full length for the first time in its life, and is looking up at the falling water. It could stay. It would only have to let go of you.

choices.text: Lie down beside it at the pool, and wait as long as it does

effects.log: A year at the pool. Two. The snake looks up at the waterfall; the tortoise looks at the snake. On the third spring the snake turns round, and looks at you instead, and comes home along your back, coil by coil, and the waterfall falls on without either of you.

choices.text: Tell it the truth: you would rather it stayed, and you will not stop it

effects.log: The snake is quiet a long time. "That is unfair," it says. "That is the only fair thing," says the tortoise. The snake winds three turns back round your shell, sulking, and stays.

choices.text: Let it go

effects.log: You feel the last coil loosen at the root, and then it is gone, and you are lighter by exactly one snake. It does not look back. You go down the mountain alone, slowly, and find a mill pond with a water wheel, and live a long life there as a plain old turtle. The children of the mill never know you were a guardian once. Some nights, in a storm, you think you hear something rising, far up the mountain, and you are glad for it, and you are not.

events.text: The tortoise is tired. It has been tired for a century. The snake argues and schemes and reads and chatters, and the tortoise draws in a little further every year. Tonight, on the bank, beside the round rock it has been looking at, the tortoise draws in both heads and does not come out. The snake, outside, alone, coils on the shell and knocks on it with its nose.

choices.text: Come out, for the snake's sake

effects.log: You put out the old slow head. The snake, outside, has been knocking for nine days and is furious and frightened and very glad. It tells you so for a month. You listen to every word.

choices.text: Open the shell and let the snake come in with you

effects.log: It has never been inside the shell. Nobody has. It is dark and close and smells of river silt and old patience. The snake coils up in there with the tortoise all winter, and in spring they come out together, and the bank is greener than it was.

choices.text: Stay in. Wait it out

effects.log: You stay in. Outside, the snake knocks for a year, and then more softly, and then not at all, and withers on the shell like a dry vine. You wait it out, and never come out. The moss comes. The villages find a turtle-shaped rock on the riverbank and tie a straw rope round it and leave paper offerings, and bow to it at the New Year, and call it Turtle Rock. You hear them, every year. It is very quiet in the shell.

events.text: The heads are pulling apart, and neither is much ahead of the other: it is not that one has outgrown the other. It is only that they have stopped talking. The snake lies along one side of the riverbed, the tortoise along the other, joined at the root, a pebble's width between them that feels like a river.

choices.text: Play stones on the riverbed until one of you laughs

effects.log: Black pebbles and white, all autumn. The snake cheats. The tortoise lets it. On the ninetieth game the tortoise cheats, badly, and the snake laughs so hard it chokes, and the pebble's width closes.

choices.text: Go on a long journey together, nowhere in particular

effects.log: Down to the sea and back. The tortoise picks the road; the snake picks the inns. By the time you are home you have quarrelled about everything twice, which is how you know it is mended. (-5 health)

events.text: A dynasty in its last years wants to know how long it has. The royal diviners have read every shell in the kingdom and every one says something different. They want the oldest shell there is. A hundred boats come up your river with nets of iron chain, and the court diviner {npc} stands in the first boat with a brazier already lit, so as not to waste time.

choices.text: Go north under the ice where the boats cannot follow

effects.log: Three seasons under the ice of the far north, while the boats wait at the edge of it and freeze into it, one by one. The diviners go home in spring on foot. They will come back. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let the snake sink the first boat

effects.log: The first boat goes over, brazier and all, with a great hiss of steam. {npc} swims ashore, and stands on the bank dripping, and looks at the river with the eyes of someone who has just been told the answer to a question.

choices.text: Rise beside {npc}'s boat and look at the brazier

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, and at the brazier, and says, very quietly, "Oh." The boats turn back. That night the diviner writes to the court that the oldest shell in the kingdom is alive and watching, and that this is, in itself, a reading.

events.text: They came back with more chain. You are in a palace hall, in a net of iron, on a stone floor, and the bronze brazier is being heated until it glows. {npc} kneels before it with brushes and paper. "I am sorry," says the diviner, and means it. "The dynasty needs to know. Every reading of your shell will be true; that is why it must be yours."

choices.text: Draw both heads in, and be cold

effects.log: You draw in and become a stone with a thousand winters in it. They heat the brazier for nine days and the shell will not warm; the frost creeps up the bronze instead. On the tenth night {npc}, grey with fear, tells the court the shell is dead, and has it thrown in the river. The river takes you home. (-20 health)

choices.text: Let the snake bargain: one true reading, freely given, for your release

ok.log: The snake reads the brazier's smoke for them, freely, truly: the dynasty has forty years, and then a good one comes. {npc} writes it down and weeps and unlocks the chain. "It keeps its word," the diviner tells the court. "That is worth more than its shell."

fail.log: The court will not bargain with a turtle. The shell is set on the brazier for one hour before a terrified {npc} kicks it over and lets you go in the night. One plate is scorched black. It does not crack. Next time, it might. (-15 health)

choices.text: Break the chain

ok.log: Both heads at once, and the iron goes like straw. You walk out of the palace through the front gate, slowly, and nobody stops you. The brazier is never lit for a turtle again in that dynasty.

fail.log: The chain holds. They beat the snake back into the shell with poles and put the shell on the coals for a night, and only a fire in the east wing saves you. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: the diviners' brazier, in a net of iron chain

choices.text: Let them read you

effects.log: They heat the shell until it cracks, plate by plate, the stars on it going out one by one. Every crack is read and written down. Every reading is true. The dynasty that took you lasts two hundred years more, and knows every year of it in advance, and is not happier for knowing. Your shell stays in the treasury, cracked and priceless, and the diviners of every later court come to look at it, and do not dare to touch it.

events.text: The dynasty that hunted you is gone, as dynasties go. In the ruins of its palace there is a bronze brazier, green with age, and a little heap of turtle plastrons beside it, cracked and written on, a thousand years of other turtles. The snake reads the cracks out of habit, and goes quiet.

choices.text: Bury them, every one, in the river mud

effects.log: A thousand shells, one by one, carried down to the river and laid in the mud. The snake reads each one before it goes. Some were right. Some were wrong. All of them were somebody.

choices.text: Let the snake read them all, to the end

effects.log: It takes a winter. At the end the snake says that the diviners were right more often than they deserved and wrong exactly when it mattered, and then it is sick in the river, which it has never been before.

events.text: The Northern seat is in sight now, on clear nights, at the edge of the sky. The snake has counted the plates on your back. Thirteen, or nearly. And some of them glow wrong. "Nobody up there was at the ford," says the snake. "Nobody saw the bride. A little lacquer: pine soot and river clay and the sap of the lacquer tree. They will see black plates and stars. Who will ever know?" The tortoise says: one will.

choices.text: Let the snake lacquer the cracks

effects.log: It takes the snake a whole autumn, a thin coat at a time, and the result is perfect. In the frost, under the lacquer, the cracks ache. The tortoise does not say anything. It does not have to.

choices.text: No. Go back and mend them, however long it takes

effects.log: The snake sighs a sigh that lasts a winter, and then starts planning the road. It knows exactly who to ask at every place. It always did.

choices.text: Ask the snake why it is in such a hurry

effects.log: "Because I am afraid you will die before we get there," says the snake, quickly, and then looks as if it wishes it had not. The tortoise has nothing to say to that, and lies close to it all winter.

events.text: A clear night, and the stair of cloud is down to the river ice: the way to the Northern seat, open for one night, as it is once in a century. Your shell is black and starred and perfect, and under the lacquer the cracked plates ache in the cold. In the centre of the sky the Yellow Dragon waits beside the empty seat, and it has, the snake notes, a very good memory and nothing else to do.

choices.text: Wash the lacquer off in the river and turn back

effects.log: You lie in the cold current all night while the lacquer softens and peels away, and the cracked plates glow wrong in the starlight for anyone to see. The stair of cloud goes back up at dawn without you. The snake does not say anything. It helps scrub.

choices.text: Climb halfway, and come back down

effects.log: Halfway up the stair you can see the seat, and the Yellow Dragon beside it, and the Yellow Dragon looks at you, only looks, and you turn round. On the river ice at dawn the snake starts scraping off the lacquer without being asked.

choices.text: Climb, with the lacquer on

effects.log: You climb all night and arrive at dawn, and the Yellow Dragon asks to read the shell before you sit. It reads aloud, plate by plate, before the whole council. At the first lacquered plate it stops, and scratches it gently with one claw, and the lacquer comes away, and the crack underneath glows red. It goes on reading. The snake cannot stop it. Plate by plate, every lie on your back is read out to the four directions. Your record is struck. You go back down the stair with your shell bare, and the north wall of the sky stays empty, and the Bird, for once, does not laugh.

events.text: A spring after the stair of cloud went up without you. The lacquer is gone, the cracks show, and the snake has been very quiet for a year. Tonight it says, without being asked: "I wrote them because it was faster. I lacquered them because I was ashamed. I would like to go and mend them now. All of them. The slow way."

choices.text: "Together, then"

effects.log: You set out in the spring, the snake leading, which is new: it knows every road to every lie it ever told, and it walks them all, and asks the old people, and listens.

choices.text: Tell the snake the tortoise was ashamed too: it let them be written

effects.log: The snake had not thought of that. It thinks of it all the way to the first ford, and is much easier to travel with.

events.text: The ice on your river melts in the middle of the twelfth month, which has never happened. Something is standing on it: a bird made of fire, every feather a flame, with a voice like a temple bell rung by a child. The Vermilion Bird of the south. "The north seat has been empty for an age," it sings, "and the council has had no clerk. I keep the minutes. I keep them very badly. I burn them, mostly. The centre says it is time somebody read your shell."

choices.text: Bow both heads to the south

effects.log: The Bird approves, and then says it has seen deeper bows, from a turtle in the Dragon King's palace, once. The snake and the Bird argue about which turtle for the rest of the afternoon, and the river refreezes round them, and you understand that this is how the south does everything.

choices.text: Let the snake ask why the minutes burn

effects.log: "Because nobody writes them true," sings the Bird, "and a false record is worse than none. So I burn them. I have burned four thousand years of them." It seems pleased with itself and also very tired. "Come and read your shell. If it is true, you can keep the next ones."

choices.text: Ask what the council will want with a tortoise

effects.log: "To read it," sings the Bird. "Everything on you, aloud. Before the north seat is filled." It looks at your back. "Bring everything. They already know most of it."

events.text: It takes a tortoise eleven years to climb into the sky, and you do it without stopping: up the stair of cloud from the north, step by slow step, the snake complaining of the height the whole way. The council terrace is vast and mostly empty. Fire in the south, the Bird. Gold in the centre, the Yellow Dragon, of earth and of the late summer between all seasons, with the patience of farmland. Three seats dark: north, east, west. In the east a blue storm hangs at the terrace edge, and in the west a white frost: the ones who will one day sit there, come to watch.

choices.text: Let the snake read your shell aloud

effects.log: The snake reads well, fast, every plate, with flourishes. The Yellow Dragon listens to all of it and then asks the tortoise if that was what happened. The tortoise says: yes, but slower.

choices.text: Let the tortoise read it, slowly

effects.log: It takes a month. The Bird falls asleep twice. The Yellow Dragon does not. At the end it says, "Thank you. Now I know how long each one took," and seems to think this is the important part.

choices.text: Read it together: the tortoise what was seen, the snake what it meant
