effects.log: The tortoise says what happened; the snake says why it mattered; neither interrupts. When it is done the Bird has stopped burning anything at all, and the Yellow Dragon says, quietly, that this is what a record is supposed to be, and that it had forgotten.

events.text: The Yellow Dragon stops the reading at the first plate you ever wrote. "Were you there?" it asks. Before the tortoise can answer, the snake does: "It was. It waited years in the mud for a stranger's ending, because I said it would come. I can lie. It cannot. Ask it anything."

choices.text: Let the tortoise answer anyway: "I was there"

effects.log: "Good," says the Yellow Dragon, and goes on to the next plate. The snake, for the rest of the reading, keeps very close to the tortoise's head, like a guard.

choices.text: Tell them about the crack that was there, and how it was mended

effects.log: The Yellow Dragon listens to the story of the mending more carefully than to any plate. "A crack mended," it says at last, "is worth two plates that never cracked. The second ones never learned anything."

choices.text: Thank the snake for defending what the tortoise saw

effects.log: The snake is so embarrassed it pretends to be reading the stars. The Bird laughs a shower of sparks and one of them lands on your shell, and the snake puts it out, and everybody pretends nothing happened.

events.text: The blue storm at the east edge of the terrace comes into the circle and is the Azure Dragon, not yet seated, sent by its own ridge to watch. It looks at your shell for a long time, at one plate in particular, and then at you. "Every autumn," it says slowly, "I dive into a deep and sleep. Every autumn something keeps that deep quiet, and every spring I rise and never know what. It is you. It was always you."

choices.text: "Somebody had to keep it quiet"

effects.log: The dragon lies down beside you on the terrace, very long, very blue, and says to the council that it will speak for the north as long as anyone likes. "Do not," says the snake, embarrassed for everyone. The Yellow Dragon writes something down.

choices.text: Let the snake tell it about the year it nearly woke

effects.log: A fisherman with a drum, a hundred years ago. The snake chased him off and the tortoise lay on the drum until spring. The dragon laughs so hard the terrace rains. The Bird is furious about the damp.

events.text: The blue storm at the east edge comes into the circle and is the Azure Dragon, not yet seated, and in no good mood. "What has the north ever given the east?" it asks the council. "Winter. Ice on my rivers, frost on my seedlings. It writes endings. I make beginnings. Why should it keep the record of the beginnings?"

choices.text: "Because every beginning you ever made came out of my winter"

effects.log: The dragon opens its mouth to answer, and does not. Somewhere in the east, at that moment, a seed that has lain all winter under your frost splits. The dragon feels it. "Fine," it says, much later. "Fine."

choices.text: Hold the winter out to it across the terrace, like a cup

effects.log: You hold the whole of the coming winter out across the terrace, cold and dark and full of sleeping seeds, the way one passes a cup across a table. The dragon looks at it a long time. Then it takes it, carefully, as if it might spill, and that is how, ever since, the year has turned.

choices.text: Let the snake answer, sharply

effects.log: The snake says several true things about dragons and humility, very fast. The dragon goes white at the whiskers. The Yellow Dragon writes the whole exchange down, which is worse than any rebuke.

events.text: The white frost at the west edge of the terrace comes into the circle and is the White Tiger, not yet seated, with stars in its stripes. It sits, and says only: "Every winter I lie down in my den and give the winter to the north. Every winter the north holds it, and gives it back clean. I have never once had to ask twice. It is worthy."

choices.text: Thank it, in front of everyone

effects.log: "Do not," says the Tiger, embarrassed, and licks a paw for a long time. The Yellow Dragon writes something down. Somewhere in the south a bird laughs.

choices.text: Tell the council about the news of the north you sent west each autumn

effects.log: The Tiger had kept every word. It produces the strips of paper, to everyone's surprise, from somewhere in its ruff. The Bird is so moved it sets them on fire, and the snake has to put them out.

events.text: The white frost at the west edge of the terrace comes into the circle and is the White Tiger, not yet seated, the judge of autumn, and it has a question. "You watched," it says. "Thirteen endings, and you watched. A house fell; a garrison burned; a woman died; a library went up. You could have acted. You wrote it down. Tell the council why a witness who could act should sit in the north."

choices.text: "Because somebody has to see it as it was"

effects.log: The Tiger weighs it the way it weighs everything, in two paws. "And when you act," it says, "who sees that?" "The snake," says the tortoise. The Tiger thinks about this for a whole season and then nods, once.

choices.text: Let the snake list the endings you changed instead

effects.log: There are more than the Tiger expected, and the snake knows the reason for each. "So you are not only a witness," says the Tiger. "No," says the snake. "That is the problem. And the gift."

choices.text: Ask the Tiger the same question about its verdicts

effects.log: The Tiger looks at you for a long time with its yellow eyes. "Fair," it says. The Yellow Dragon writes both questions down side by side and leaves them unanswered, which is the most honest thing anyone does all century.

events.text: A witness is called: {npc}, a human of the upper heavens. Once, {npc} tells the council, on a winter solstice, the seven northern mansions came down over a frozen river as a tortoise and a snake made of stars and asked {him} to keep the record of one hearing, because the council had no clerk. "I wrote the tortoise's account and the snake's side by side," {npc} says. "I wanted the council to know they did not disagree on a single fact. Only on what the facts were for."

choices.text: Let {him} read the old record aloud

effects.log: {npc} reads both columns. The tortoise's is short. The snake's is long. Where they meet, at the bottom of the page, they say the same thing in different words. The Yellow Dragon asks for a copy.

choices.text: Ask {him} which account the council should believe

effects.log: "Both," says {npc}, without hesitating. "That was the whole point. That is why it needs two heads." The snake nods as if that were the only thing that mattered, and perhaps it is.

events.text: The Bird comes and sits beside you at the edge of the terrace with an armful of minutes, the last century's, scorched at the corners. "I was going to burn these too," it says. "Every guardian who ever spoke at this council lied a little. Spring said it was humble. Autumn said it was fair. I say I am kind. Nobody could write it true, so I burned it. You could. Will you?"

choices.text: Take the minutes, and write them true, lies and all

effects.log: You write the whole scorched century onto the inside of your shell: what each guardian said, and, beside it in the snake's small hand, what each guardian meant. The Bird reads it over your shoulder and laughs until it cries sparks. "Oh, that is much worse," it says. "Keep it for ever."

choices.text: Let the Bird keep burning them, for now

effects.log: "Good," says the Bird, and sets the armful alight with a sigh of relief. The smoke goes up into the stars. The snake memorises as much as it can before it goes.

events.text: You take the north seat, and for the first time in an age the north of the sky is not dark. The Yellow Dragon rises from the centre and puts a brush in front of you on the cloud: long, black-handled, the hairs white as frost. "The council has had no clerk," it says. "Everything the four directions decide from now on is written on your back. Write the first line."

choices.text: Write: "The north was empty. Now it is not."

effects.log: The tortoise writes it slowly, the snake holding the inkstone steady. The Yellow Dragon reads it and says, "True," and sits back down. The Bird, for the first time in four thousand years, does not burn the page.

choices.text: Write the date, and the weather, and nothing else

effects.log: A clear night, a hard frost, wind from the north. The Yellow Dragon looks at it for a long time. "That is the first honest minute this council has ever had," it says.

choices.text: Write the names of every ending on your back, as a preface

effects.log: The funerals, the weddings, the roofs that fell, the roads and the bridges, the fires, the books, and all the rest. It takes all night. Nobody tells you to hurry. It is, the Bird says afterwards, the first time the council has begun with somebody else.

events.text: The east seat is still empty, and the council sends the clerk to call it. It takes a tortoise eleven years to climb a dragon's ridge, and you do it without stopping, both heads talking at once. At the top the Azure Dragon is lying along the pines. "The council of the four directions," says the tortoise. "Will hear your record," says the snake. "Before the east seat is filled," you finish together. "Bring everything. We already know it."

choices.text: Watch the dragon bow

effects.log: It bows to the north. The tortoise approves. The snake says it has seen better bows. You argue about it for the rest of the afternoon on the dragon's ridge, while the dragon waits, and the dragon understands that this is how the north does everything.

choices.text: Answer the dragon's question: what is the record for?

effects.log: "Spring cannot be trusted to an animal that does not know what it did," says the snake. "Or what it did not do," says the tortoise. At your age it seems obvious. The dragon, much younger, writes it down.

choices.text: Laugh, when it says its record will speak for itself

effects.log: "It will," says the tortoise mildly, and the snake laughs, a dry sound like ice cracking on a river. The dragon is not sure what was funny. It will find out.

events.text: The west seat is still empty, and the council sends the clerk to call it. It takes a tortoise eleven years to climb a tiger's mountain, and you do it without stopping. At the top the White Tiger is lying on a bare summit with stars in its stripes. "The council of the four directions," says the tortoise. "Will read your record," says the snake. "Before the west seat is filled," you finish together. "Bring your docket. Bring your dead."

choices.text: Accept the tiger's bow, and argue about it

effects.log: The snake says it has seen better bows, from a dragon, once. The tortoise says which dragon. You argue about which dragon for the rest of the afternoon on the summit, while the tiger waits, and the tiger understands that this is how the north does everything.

choices.text: Tell the tiger, when it says it keeps no record but its teeth, that you will read its teeth

effects.log: "Then we will read your teeth," says the tortoise mildly, and the snake laughs, a dry sound like ice cracking on a river. The tiger shuts its mouth very carefully.

choices.text: Explain, when it asks, why the judge must be judged first

effects.log: "Autumn judges every living thing," says the snake. "So the one who keeps autumn," says the tortoise, "must have been judged first." The tiger considers this for a long time and finds it, grudgingly, fair.

events.text: Your record is open on the terrace for the dragon's hearing, and the Azure Dragon and the Vermilion Bird bow to each other at the same moment and bang heads, gently. The Bird laughs so hard that it sets fire to your record. The page in question is the inside of your own shell.

choices.text: Let the snake put it out

effects.log: The snake smothers the flames with its own coils, hissing, and is singed down one side for a year. The council adjourns for a day. The Bird sends an apology in the form of a very warm summer for the north, which nobody there wanted.

choices.text: Do nothing. The tortoise has been burned before

effects.log: You sit perfectly still while the edge of a plate smoulders and goes out on its own. The Bird stops laughing. "You are no fun," it says, and then, "I am sorry," and means both.

choices.text: Write down that the Bird set fire to the minutes again

effects.log: You write it down, with the date. The Bird reads it and is outraged and then delighted. It is the first time it has ever been in the minutes. It asks for a copy.

events.text: A quarrel in the council. The south wants a long hot summer for the rice; the east wants a wet spring; the west wants an early autumn for its orchards. And the north, which is you, wants a hard early frost, because the snake has read the locust eggs in the soil of three provinces and the tortoise knows what a locust year does to the poor. The Yellow Dragon in the middle has declined to have an opinion and is pretending to sleep.

choices.text: Send word to the west to bring the harvest forward, and freeze on time

effects.log: The west brings the harvest forward a month in one great breath. The last sheaf is in the barn the evening before your frost. Every locust egg in three provinces dies. You send one word west: "Neat."

choices.text: Wait a month for the rice, and freeze late and hard

effects.log: The rice finishes. Your frost comes the week after, all at once, and the locust eggs die. The south is nearly satisfied, the west is cross, and nobody can prove whose idea it was.

choices.text: Write the quarrel down and let the others fight it out

effects.log: The fight is spectacular and lasts a week. You write every word. The weather that year is very strange, and the Yellow Dragon, who was not asleep at all, reads your minutes afterwards and laughs for the first time in a millennium.

events.text: Your first hearing as clerk. A kingdom has fallen in the world below, and its guardian, a mountain god in a white beard, stands before the council and says it could not have been saved. The Yellow Dragon turns to you: the record of this hearing is yours to keep. The tortoise wants to write what was seen. The snake wants to write what was meant.

choices.text: Write the tortoise's account: what was seen

effects.log: The famine, the war, the king who would not listen, the god who tried. All of it, slowly, nothing added. The mountain god reads it and weeps: it is exactly as it was, and it is not kind.

choices.text: Write the snake's account: what was meant

effects.log: The god meant well; the king meant to; the war meant nothing to anybody. The mountain god reads it and is comforted, and the Yellow Dragon reads it and asks, gently, where the facts are.

choices.text: Write both, side by side

effects.log: Two columns, the tortoise's short and the snake's long, meeting at the bottom of the plate. The mountain god reads both, and is neither comforted nor condemned, only understood. The Yellow Dragon has the page copied and hung in the centre of the sky.

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court arrives at the council terrace with a retinue of clerks and a mandate to audit the four guardians: winds, rains, harvests, verdicts, every century accounted for. You produce your shell. The Bird produces a song. The Azure Dragon produces its seven stars. The envoy turns to the west, and the White Tiger lays a fine red deer at the envoy's feet, freshly killed. The clerks stop writing. "That is not what was asked for," says the envoy. "It is what the west has," says the Tiger.

choices.text: Laugh out loud, with both heads

effects.log: Both heads, at once, the tortoise's slow boom and the snake's dry crackle, and nobody on the terrace has ever heard the north laugh before. The envoy looks at you. The Tiger looks pleased with itself. The audit never quite recovers its dignity.

choices.text: Keep a straight face, and write in your minutes: Deer, one. Received.

effects.log: You write it in your neatest characters. The envoy reads it over your shoulder, and something happens to its face, and it has to go and stand at the edge of the terrace for a while looking at the clouds.

events.text: The envoy audits the north for a decade. It reads your shell plate by plate, every ending and every word, and then the minutes of the council since you took the brush. It reads slowly. It is the first auditor in four thousand years with anything to read.

choices.text: Answer every question, however small

effects.log: The envoy asks about the oldest plate, the smallest, the one that took the longest. You know every answer. At the end it closes its ledger and says, "The north is in order," and then, more quietly, "The north is the only thing in order."

choices.text: Let the snake show the envoy the places where the snake was wrong

effects.log: The mended cracks, the changed words, the omens it read badly. The snake shows every one. The envoy writes them down with great care and adds, in red, that this is the first guardian to audit itself.

events.text: The audit is concluded. The envoy is packing its ledgers. The Azure Dragon, who has been waiting a decade for its chance, asks the envoy, very politely, who audits the Jade court. The envoy goes very still. The clerks stop packing.

choices.text: Laugh out loud with both heads, again

effects.log: To everyone's surprise, including your own, the north laughs again. The envoy leaves an hour early. The dragon looks at you sideways for the rest of the century, delighted to have an accomplice.

choices.text: Answer, as clerk: "The record does"

effects.log: The envoy looks at your shell for a long moment, and then bows to it, which nobody has ever seen a Jade court envoy do, and takes a copy of your minutes back to the Jade court, where, the Bird reports later, they are causing trouble.

events.text: Two hundred years later, a new envoy, a new audit. This one has read the old ledger first. It stands on the council terrace, looks at the White Tiger, and says carefully: "I have been asked to ask the west not to bring a deer." The Tiger considers this, and lays a boar at its feet.

choices.text: Laugh until the snake has to help you back onto your feet

effects.log: You laugh so hard you go over onto your back, which for a tortoise the size of a threshing floor is serious, and the snake has to brace itself against the cloud and heave you upright. The envoy writes it down with a perfectly straight face. Boar, one.

choices.text: Write it in your minutes, beside the deer

effects.log: Deer, one. Received. Two hundred years later: Boar, one. Received. The two lines sit together on the inside of your shell for ever, and every guardian who reads them has to stop for a moment and look at the clouds.

events.text: The Northern Palace is not one hall but seven, in a line along the cloud like the mansions they are named for. The Dipper, where the register of years is kept. The Ox, where every road and bridge is mapped. The Girl, with its looms. Emptiness, where the weeping is. Rooftop, the treasury. Encampment, the granaries of heaven. And at the end the Wall: heaven's secret archive of books, every book ever lost. They have been shut for an age. The keys are on your back.
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the North

choices.text: Walk all seven before you sit

effects.log: A whole year, one hall after another, both heads looking. The dust in the Dipper hall is a thousand years deep. The looms in the Girl hall still have work on them, half woven. In Emptiness someone is still weeping, very quietly, and has been for an age. You sit at last at the end of the line knowing the shape of the whole north.

choices.text: Go straight to the Wall

effects.log: The snake cannot help it. Every book ever lost: the snake reads titles aloud in the dark between the shelves until its voice goes, and the tortoise follows behind, putting back the ones it pulled out.

events.text: The hall of the Dipper. On a stand in the middle, a register of years: every life, and how long. Two cushions are set before it, worn into the shape of two old men who sat there a long time and are not there now. On the open page, among the villages and the years, a nineteen crossed out, and a ninety-nine written over it in a different hand.
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the North

choices.text: Read the page, and leave it as it is

effects.log: You read the whole page: a village, a generation, every number. Some were changed. Most were not. You turn no pages and change nothing, and when you go, the two cushions seem, very slightly, to approve.

choices.text: Let the snake look up its own entry

effects.log: It finds it. It reads it. It does not tell the tortoise what it says. For a week it is unusually kind to everyone, and then it is itself again.

choices.text: Sit on the cushions, one head on each, for an hour

effects.log: One soft cushion, one hard. The snake gets the hard one and says it is perfect. For an hour the hall of the Dipper has its keepers again, and somewhere in the world below a sick child sleeps through the night.

events.text: The hall of Emptiness, where the weeping is. Someone has been weeping here for an age: a woman of the world below, or the shade of one, kneeling by an empty bier. Nobody ever buried her son. He died in a war four hundred years ago on a river you know, and she has been waiting in heaven's hall of mourning for someone to tell her where.
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the North

choices.text: Tell her: you saw where. You were there

effects.log: You were under the ice when the black flags crossed. You saw a boy go through. You tell her the bend, the willow, the stone. She gets up for the first time in four hundred years, and bows, and walks out of the hall of Emptiness, and it is quiet in there for the first time since it was built.

choices.text: Go down to the river and bring him up

effects.log: It takes a year to find the bones under four centuries of silt. You carry them up the stair of cloud on your back and lay them on the empty bier. She stops weeping. You both sit there a long time. (-12 health)

events.text: The hall of the Wall, heaven's archive of lost books. On a shelf at eye level, as if someone left it out for you: the woodblocks of the temple library that burned, every one that burned, whole, the smell of smoke still on them. And beside them, a gap where four thousand blocks should be: the ones you carried out, which were never lost, and so never came here.
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the North

choices.text: Touch the gap, and be glad

effects.log: Four thousand blocks still in the world below, being printed from, being worn down by hands. The gap on heaven's shelf is the best thing in the archive. The snake says so. The tortoise agrees.

choices.text: Read the burned ones, all of them

effects.log: A whole decade among the racks, reading what burned. The snake turns the pages. When you finish you can recite the catalogue, and you know what each title meant.

events.text: A petitioner in the hall of the Ox, where every road and bridge is mapped: a ferry spirit from a river you do not know, whose ferry has been replaced by a bridge, and who does not know what to do with forever now. It has come to the north because the north is where endings are kept.
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the North

choices.text: Find it a new crossing on the map

effects.log: There is a river in the far west with no ferry and a village on each bank that have never met. The spirit goes there. Fifty years later the two villages hold a joint wedding every spring.

choices.text: Tell it an ending is allowed to be an ending

effects.log: It thinks about this a long time, in the hall of the Ox, and then goes down to its old river and lies under the new bridge and sleeps, content, and the bridge never once floods.

choices.text: Let the snake hire it as a messenger for the council

effects.log: It turns out a ferry spirit is very good at carrying things across. The council's minutes have never moved so fast. The Bird is horrified.

events.text: Four thousand years of minutes burned by the Bird, and the council asks you to make good the gap, as far as you can. You were not there for most of it. The snake says it can reconstruct a great deal from what everyone remembers, and what everyone remembers is mostly flattering.

choices.text: Write only what you witnessed, and leave the rest blank

effects.log: Four thousand years, and you can honestly fill eleven pages. The rest of the record is blank, and you label it: burned, not known. The Yellow Dragon says it has never seen a more beautiful gap.

choices.text: Let the snake reconstruct it, marked as reconstructed

effects.log: The snake reconstructs four thousand years in a decade, and marks every line it did not see with a small black triangle. There are a great many triangles. It is the most useful history of heaven ever written, and the most honest about itself.

choices.text: Let the snake reconstruct it, unmarked

effects.log: It reads beautifully. It is mostly true. The tortoise says nothing, and the inside of your shell aches faintly in the cold all century, the way a cracked plate used to.

events.text: A hearing on the Azure Dragon: in a dry year, long ago, it took the rain first and left the west what was over. The Dragon has confessed it, well and humbly. The snake, holding the inkstone, suggests that the record need not mention the part where the Dragon roared at the Tiger first. The Dragon has been very good lately.

choices.text: Write all of it, the roar too

effects.log: All of it. The Dragon reads it and winces at the roar and then says, "Yes. That is what I did." Afterwards it is a little cooler to you for a decade, and a little more careful with everyone.

choices.text: Leave out the roar, as a kindness

effects.log: The Dragon never knows. The Tiger does, and says nothing, and looks at your shell a long time the next time it passes.

choices.text: Write the roar, and beside it, in the snake's hand, why

effects.log: The roar, and the drought, and the dying valley it was roaring for. The Dragon reads it and is understood rather than excused, which is rarer. The Tiger reads it and nods.

events.text: A human scribe climbs to the council terrace, which almost no human does: {npc}, the last archivist of a dynasty that burned its own records rather than let the conqueror have them. {He} has walked up the stair of cloud with nothing but a brush. "The clerk of heaven," {he} says. "Teach me to write things down so they cannot be burned."

choices.text: Teach {him} to write on memory: tell it to a hundred people

effects.log: {npc} goes down the stair and tells the dynasty's history to a hundred children in a hundred villages, and makes each one tell it back. Three hundred years later it is still being told, a little wrong, entirely unburnable.

choices.text: Let {him} copy a page of your shell

effects.log: One page: the endings of a burned library and a fallen house. {npc} copies it in a fair hand and takes it down into the world, and builds an archive around it, of stone, by a river, and calls it the North Wall.

choices.text: Tell {him} that everything burns, and that is why it must be written

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time, then at the brush in {his} own hand. "Then I will write it again," {he} says, "every time." It is the right answer. You let {him} stay a year on the terrace and watch you work.

events.text: You have run out of room. Thirteen plates and the whole inside of the shell are written edge to edge, the four directions' minutes for centuries, in the tortoise's large slow hand and the snake's small quick one. The Yellow Dragon looks at it and says that clerks in the old days used to grow.

choices.text: Grow

effects.log: It takes a century, and it is not comfortable. At the end your shell is wider by a third, and the new plates are pale and blank and smell of snow, and the snake is already sharpening the brush.

choices.text: Start writing smaller

effects.log: The snake can write a whole hearing on a plate the size of a coin. The tortoise cannot read it. They agree that the tortoise will dictate and the snake will write, which is how it should always have been, and the minutes improve.

events.text: A great gut on a hillside at the winter solstice: a mudang in robes of the five colours, two drummers, a cymbal player, and five long flags on bamboo poles, blue, red, white, black, yellow. The mudang turns to each direction and calls its emperor down: the Blue Emperor of the east, the Red Emperor of the south, the White Emperor of the west, the Yellow Emperor of the centre. Then the mudang spins north, with a black fan and a bell, and stops dead, facing you.

choices.text: Come down into the black flag

effects.log: The black silk fills on a windless night, heavy as a sail full of snow, and the mudang staggers, laughing, and the drummers lose the beat. Every pond on the hillside freezes at once with a sound like a bell. The village will talk of nothing else until spring.

choices.text: Come as the north wind only, and let the rite go on

effects.log: A long cold breath goes once round the hill, through the black flag and away. The mudang feels it and finishes the rite as if nothing happened, which is how the best of them do it.

choices.text: You are a tortoise, not an emperor. Stay in the river

effects.log: The mudang calls three times, then smiling moves on. The black flag hangs still. Winter comes anyway, a little late, and nobody minds.

events.text: After the rite the mudang lets the village pick its fortune from the five flags, rolled tight on their poles: pull one blind, and the colour tells the year. A small child, {npc}, has pulled the black flag five winters running, and the mudang has started to look north thoughtfully while {he} does it. Black is not a lucky colour. The child does not seem to mind.

choices.text: Let {him} pull black again

mem.note: gave me the black flag every winter

effects.log: Six winters. Then seven. Every one of them, the child's family has the warmest house in the village, and nobody understands why. When {npc} is grown the mudang takes the child of the black flag as an apprentice, and the valley has a mudang of its own who never once has to call the north twice.

choices.text: Let {him} pull yellow this year, so the world does not seem arranged for one child

effects.log: Yellow: a middling year, a dull one. {npc} is outraged, then shrugs, then pulls black again the next winter and is much less surprised about it.

events.text: An old god comes to you on the frozen river, the one the ice rites were always made to: the north god who governs cold, thin as an icicle, in robes the colour of a winter night, carrying a peach-wood bow with no string. It kneels, which you did not know gods did. "I have kept the cold for the ice houses since the first king," it says. "Nobody answers my rite any more. They answer yours. I would like, if the Black Emperor permits, to rest."

choices.text: Take the bow, and give it back to the old god to carry

effects.log: The bow is very light and very cold. You hold it a moment and hand it back. "Carry it," says the tortoise. "Use it seldom," says the snake. The old god bows lower, and from then on walks a pace behind you, everywhere, and the frost walks with it.

choices.text: Tell it to lie down and rest a century

effects.log: The old god looks at the bow as if it had never thought of putting it down. Then it does, on the river ice, and lies down beside it, and sleeps a hundred years under the snow. That century the winters come gently, and the ice houses are full anyway.

events.text: The longest night of the year, and the Northern Dipper stands on its handle over the pole, the seven stars that keep the register of death, turning round the one star that never moves. For the first time you can feel the whole northern sky from the inside, the way you feel your own two heads.

choices.text: Turn the Dipper one notch, slowly, as the year turns

effects.log: The handle swings, very slowly, over every house in the north. In the world below, every child awake that night looks up at the same moment, and nobody can say why.

choices.text: Go on being a tortoise on the ice, watching it

effects.log: You watch your own sky turn over the river like any ferryman. It is very beautiful. It is very far away. You are not ready for it to be you, and the snake, for once, agrees.

events.text: The Jade court sends for you. Beyond the four directions there is a world that has never had a winter: no rest, no fallow, no sleep. Its fields are worked to dust; its trees fruit until they die; its people have forgotten how to stop. "The Black Emperor of the North," says the envoy, "is asked to carry winter there. It is a long way. You may not come back the same."

choices.text: Go, and carry winter

effects.log: It takes a century. Field by field, house by house, you breathe on a world that could not rest, until the trees drop their leaves and the fields lie under snow and the people, astonished, sleep. You come home thinner, and lighter, and somehow larger.

choices.text: Send the north wind, and stay with your own rivers

effects.log: The wind goes alone across the dark between worlds and arrives tired. The winter there is thin, but it comes, and that is more than they had.

choices.text: Ask why heaven let it go without rest

effects.log: The envoy does not answer for a long time. "Because nobody would let it stop," it says at last. "That is usually why." You do not go that century. You think about it every winter after.

events.text: The winter rite on the hill, as every year since the black flag first filled. The mudang is the great-great-grandchild of the child who pulled the black flag, or someone very like them. They spin north with the black fan and the bell, and stop dead, facing you. And this time you feel it all the way through: if you answer, you will answer as winter, and not come back as a tortoise. The flag waits. The drums wait. Every sleeping thing in the land waits.

choices.text: Answer as winter

effects.log: You let go of the river, the plates, the brush, the shell, the name, and the snake lets go with you, at exactly the same moment, for once without arguing. The black flag fills. Snow comes down over the whole land at once, soft and deep. There is no tortoise on the river any more. There is only winter, every winter, for ever: every winter your breath held, every thaw your breath let go. The mudang on the hill, weeping and laughing, is the first to feel it.

choices.text: Answer as a tortoise, one more time

effects.log: You come down into the black flag as you did a thousand years ago, a tortoise and a snake, and the mudang staggers under the weight and laughs, and the village sees you whole. There will be another winter for the other answer.

choices.text: Let the mudang call, and stay still, and listen

effects.log: Three calls. You listen to all three, both heads. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard: a human voice calling winter by its name. Winter comes anyway, from somewhere inside you, without your having to decide.

events.text: The winter solstice on the hill, the drums, the five flags, the mudang spinning north. Another year of the rite. The faces in the crowd change every generation; the rite does not. A grandmother holds a baby up toward the black flag so the Black Emperor can see it, and the baby sneezes.

choices.text: Bless the baby

effects.log: A cold clean breath, smelling of snow, ruffles the baby's hair. It sneezes again. The grandmother is satisfied. That child will never once, in a long life, be cold at night.

choices.text: Bless the whole hill

effects.log: Snow comes down on the hill in the windless dark, soft as feathers, and every pot of red-bean porridge on every doorstep stays warm until dawn. The mudang, who has seen this before, simply waits, smiling, until the drummers find the beat again.

events.text: You notice, one year, that you cannot find the edge of yourself. The ice on every river is you. The snow on the roofs, the frost on the inside of the paper doors, the deep sleep of every frog in every pond: you, all of it, everywhere at once. On the near side of the year the White Tiger of the west is holding out the autumn to you, harvested and finished, and waiting for you to take it into the dark.

choices.text: Take the year from the Tiger, and nod both heads

effects.log: Autumn goes into you and comes out winter. It is not a thing you do; it is a thing that happens through you, as ice happens on a pond. You nod both heads and take the year into the dark, and the Tiger goes back west, satisfied, to sleep.

choices.text: Pull yourself back into one shell, for now

effects.log: You gather it all up, the ice, the snow, the sleep, back into one shell on one river. It feels small. It feels like home. Winter that year is a little late, and very local.

events.text: The turn of the year. On the far side of the dark the Azure Dragon is waiting, as it does every year now, at the place where winter becomes spring, and you hold the winter out to it across the year, like a cup handed across a table, full of sleeping seeds.

choices.text: Hand it over, carefully, so nothing spills

effects.log: The dragon takes the cup, and drinks, and goes green. Somewhere in the east the first plum opens on a frozen branch. You go back north to wait for autumn.

choices.text: Hold it one more day, because the seed rice is not ready

effects.log: One more day of frost. The dragon waits, puzzled, then sees why. The seed rice in ten thousand storehouses finishes its sleep. Spring comes a day late and is better for it.

events.text: Spring is tired. You can feel it on the far side of the year: the Azure Dragon, a thousand years of beginnings, not wanting to begin again. It sends no message. It does not have to. The ice stays on the paddies a day too long.

choices.text: Hold winter a week longer, carefully, so that nothing dies

effects.log: "Everybody gets tired," says the tortoise. "Even spring," says the snake. A week of soft frost, light enough that no seedling dies, while somewhere in the east a dragon sleeps in. When it comes, it comes gratefully.

choices.text: Let go on time. Spring will come when it comes

effects.log: You let the year go on time. The ice goes grey, then black. Spring comes a week late, heavily, like an old farmer getting up before dawn, and the very old women of the villages say it is tired this year, and leave out extra rice.

events.text: The first ice of the year on a village pond, and the children of the village are on it before it is ready, as children are, sliding in their padded jackets. One of them goes out too far. You feel the ice give under one small foot the way you feel a word catch in a throat.

choices.text: Hold the ice

effects.log: The ice holds where it should not. The child slides back to the bank laughing, never knowing. Three ponds over, a fourth child goes through a patch you did not see. Every winter you will have to choose where to look.

choices.text: Hold every pond in the land at once, for one afternoon

effects.log: Every pond in the land is solid as stone for one afternoon, and not one child goes through, anywhere. It costs you something you cannot name. It is worth it.

events.text: The winter solstice, the longest night. In every house in the land someone is stirring a pot of red-bean porridge, with little balls of glutinous rice in it, one for every year of every person's age, and flicking a spoonful at the gate and the walls to keep the bad spirits off. The smell of it rises through the snow into you.

choices.text: Keep the night long and still, so the bad spirits stay away

effects.log: The longest night is the stillest in a century. No ghost walks anywhere. In ten thousand houses the old count the rice balls in their bowls, and are not afraid of the number.

choices.text: Let the snake count the rice balls in every bowl

effects.log: It counts them all, every bowl in the land, every year of every life, and then reads the total aloud to the tortoise, who falls asleep halfway, and the snake finishes it anyway.

events.text: A famine winter in the south: the rice failed, the granaries are empty, and every extra day of cold is a day somebody old does not see. The council has asked nothing. You could shorten the winter. Then the locust eggs in the soil would live, and the next harvest would fail too.

choices.text: Shorten it, and send word to the west to harvest early next year

effects.log: Nine days off the winter. Nine days is a lot of old people. The locusts come next summer, and the White Tiger brings the harvest forward a month in one great breath, and you send it one word: "Neat."

choices.text: Keep it full length. The snake asks who pays; the tortoise answers

effects.log: The tortoise answers: the old, this winter. Or everyone, next. You keep the winter. You feel every one of them go, and you write each one down. (-5 health)

choices.text: Keep it full length over the fields, and mild over the houses

effects.log: Hard frost in the soil, soft air round the eaves. It is very difficult, and very tiring, and nobody ever knows it was done. The locust eggs die. The old people mostly live.

events.text: Everything that sleeps in winter sleeps in you now: the bears in their dens, the frogs in the mud, the snakes in their knots under the stones, the seeds, the bulbs, the turtles under the ice of ten thousand ponds. A great breathing quiet. The snake can hear every one of them dreaming.

choices.text: Let the snake listen to their dreams

effects.log: The bears dream of honey. The frogs dream of nothing at all. The snakes dream of being dragons. The turtles, every one of them, dream of being two.

choices.text: Lie still, and sleep with them, one winter

effects.log: For one winter the Black Emperor of the North sleeps like a pond turtle, both heads tucked in, and the world goes on being winter without you having to think about it. You wake at the thaw better rested than you have been in a thousand years.

events.text: Every grave on every hill is under the snow, which is you. Some of them are very old: a stone causeway nobody crosses any more, a tomb with a painted wall, a mound by a ford where an old woman was buried who died telling a story. Nobody visits those in winter.

choices.text: Go to them yourself, every winter

effects.log: Every winter a clean cold wind goes over the old graves and lays the snow smooth on them, like a sheet tucked in. It is the least you can do. It is, you think, also the most.

choices.text: Write their names on the ice of the river, every winter, and let the thaw take them

effects.log: Every winter the river freezes with names in it, in two hands, one large and slow and one small and quick. Every spring they go down to the sea. The fishermen at the river mouth say the spring ice talks.

events.text: Generations of being winter, and the snake asks the tortoise a question it has never asked: whether, of all of it, the tortoise would have had it any other way. The two heads are face to face on the ice of the far north under the aurora, as they have been since the Black Warrior, and the tortoise takes a very long time to answer.

choices.text: "No"

effects.log: "No," says the tortoise. "Not one plate." The snake is quiet. Then it says it would have changed four, and names them, and the tortoise says that is why there were two of you. They lie on the ice until dawn.

choices.text: "Yes. One of them. I should have acted sooner"

effects.log: The snake is astonished. In two thousand years the tortoise has never once wished it had acted faster. "I have been rubbing off on you," it says. "Yes," says the tortoise. "Thank you."

choices.text: Ask the snake the same question

effects.log: "Every one," says the snake at once. Then, much more slowly: "And none of them. Because then it would not be us." It is the slowest thing the snake has ever said, and the tortoise is very proud of it.

events.text: You find yourself, without meaning to come, at a bend in a northern river where the bank is black sand. You know it by the cold of the water and the shape of the bend. Under the frost on the sand, a turtle has laid her eggs this autumn, and in one of them, you can feel it through the sand, there are two hearts beating out of time.

choices.text: Lie in the shallows and listen until dark

effects.log: A slow heart and a quick one, already arguing. You listen until the stars come out. You go before they hatch, because you remember how confusing it was, and do not want to make it worse.

choices.text: Keep the herons off the bank all spring

effects.log: The snake does it, mostly, with great enthusiasm. In spring the eggs hatch and the hatchlings go down to the water, and one of them is tangled, and you do not follow it. That was always the point.

events.text: An old grey crane is standing on one leg in the shallows of the black-sand bank: the crane of the ten long-lived things, who bet you once it would outlive you and has been waiting a thousand years to collect. It is not joking today. "Some go to the sky," it says. "Some into a wall, or a hill, or a stone. A few, a very few, ask to go back to the black sand and do it all again, both hearts, remembering every plate. It is allowed. It is not encouraged. I was asked to tell you."

choices.text: Ask why anyone would choose it

effects.log: "To write it better," says the crane. "Or to see if it comes out the same. Or because the first winter under the ice was the best one." It shifts to the other leg. "Turtles are sentimental. Nobody believes it, but it is so."

choices.text: Ask whether the heads would remember each other

effects.log: "Every argument," says the crane. "From the egg." The snake says that sounds terrible. The tortoise says it sounds wonderful. The crane says that settles it, and flies off, and you are not sure what it settled.

events.text: Another autumn, the first frost. The crane is on one leg in the shallows. The black-sand bank is empty this year, waiting. Behind you the whole northern sky is lit; ahead of you is a hollow in black sand, dark and cold and smelling of the river. "Well?" says the crane.

choices.text: Lie down on the bank, and stay what you are

effects.log: You lie on the black sand until the frost covers you, and then you get up and shake it off and go north. "Next frost, then," says the crane, which never takes no for an answer either.

choices.text: Go into the sand

effects.log: You go down, and in, and it gets very small and very dark and very close, and then there are two hearts in one egg, a slow one and a quick one, beating out of time, and both of them remember everything. Outside, in the first frost, a crane stands on one leg and watches the sand, and wins its bet, and does not feel like it won.

events.text: A grandmaster of the murim, {npc}, has walked out onto your frozen river in the dark with a sword and a lantern. "The Black Warrior of the north," {he} says, delighted. "I have beaten every sword in the realm. I would like to lose to you, once, before I die." The snake rises out of the shell and looks at {him}. The tortoise looks at {him}. "Which of us?" they ask together.

choices.text: "Both of us"

ok.log: It is the best fight in three hundred years. {npc} can read one head; nobody can read two. When it is over {npc} lies on the ice laughing with a broken sword. "Two," {he} says. "Of course. Thank you. Now I know what is at the top."

fail.log: {npc} is better than anyone has a right to be. Neither of you wins. {He} goes back over the ice bleeding and overjoyed, and you lie under it thinking that humans are much stranger than turtles. (-20 health)

choices.text: Send the snake alone

effects.log: The snake and {npc} fight for an hour on the ice, very fast, and call it a draw by agreement, and then sit and talk technique until dawn while the tortoise sleeps.

choices.text: Send the tortoise alone, and let {him} tire

effects.log: The tortoise does nothing at all, for a day and a night, while {npc} strikes the shell with every form {he} knows. At dawn {npc} sits down on the ice and laughs. "That is the most I have ever learned from losing," {he} says.

events.text: A human who has climbed to your level, which almost no human does: {npc}, an immortal of a great age, sits down on the river ice across from you as if it were a bench in a market. "Everyone writes about me," {he} says. "Songs, chronicles, sect histories. All lies, some kind and some not. I would like one true record before I go wherever immortals go. Will you write me down?"

choices.text: Write {him} down truthfully, everything, the bad years too

mem.note: was written down truly by the Black Tortoise

effects.log: It takes a decade on the ice. {npc} tells it all, and the snake asks the questions {he} did not want asked. At the end there is one plate-side of small characters. {npc} reads it and is quiet a long time. "Yes," {he} says. "That was me." It is the happiest you have ever seen a human.

choices.text: Let the snake write {him} kindly

effects.log: The snake writes beautifully. {npc} reads it and smiles and thanks you, and then, at the edge of the ice, turns back. "That was very kind," {he} says. "I asked for true." The tortoise had said so.

events.text: A heavenly immortal stops you on the stair of cloud: {npc}, in robes of white cloud, who bows very low. "You will not remember me," {he} says. "Long ago, a youth who was to die at nineteen climbed a mountain with a jar and a strip of venison, to two old men at baduk. A black tortoise came up the path behind me. I was frightened of it. I wanted to say that I lived. All ninety-nine."

choices.text: Say you remember

effects.log: You do: the jar, the kneeling, the snake arguing. {npc} weeps, and then laughs, and the three of you walk up the stair of cloud together talking about a mountain that is not there any more.

choices.text: Ask what {he} did with the eighty extra years

effects.log: "Charcoal, for forty," says {npc}. "Then a physician, for thirty. Then a hermit. Then this." {He} gestures at the cloud robes. "It all started with nineteen being crossed out." The snake says it argued for that. {npc} bows to the snake separately.

events.text: An immortal sovereign sends an envoy, and then comes in person: {npc}, ruler of a court in the high heavens, who wants the north. Not the cold; the records. "Everything the Four Guardians decide is written on your back," {he} says pleasantly. "Who rules the record rules the council. Come to my court. You would want for nothing. You would only write what I say."

choices.text: Tell {him} the record is not for sale, both heads at once

effects.log: {npc} smiles and goes. That winter {his} court's rivers, and only those, freeze to the bottom. The next envoy is much more polite.

choices.text: Write down the offer, word for word, in front of {him}

effects.log: {npc} watches the brush move, and reads {his} own words on your shell, with the date and the hour, in the record of the Four Guardians for ever. {He} leaves very quickly and never comes back.

choices.text: Let the snake pretend to consider it, to learn what the court wants

effects.log: The snake learns a great deal in a season of pretending. The council is very interested in all of it. The tortoise does not enjoy the pretending, and says so, every day.

events.text: A historian of the capital, {npc}, comes down to your river with a hundred questions written on a scroll. Every court chronicle of the last five hundred years contradicts every other. "They say the black tortoise of the north was there for all of it," {he} says, not quite believing it. "I would like to know what actually happened."

choices.text: Answer every question, one per day, for a hundred days

effects.log: A hundred days on the riverbank. {npc} writes until {his} hand cramps. The chronicle {he} writes afterwards is so dull, so careful and so exactly right that the court refuses to publish it, and it is copied secretly by every scholar in the kingdom for three hundred years.

choices.text: Answer only the questions you witnessed, and say so

effects.log: Twenty-three of the hundred. For the rest, the tortoise says, "I was not there," every time, until {npc} starts laughing. "Do you know," {he} says, "that no source in five hundred years has ever once said that?"

choices.text: Let the snake answer, colourfully

effects.log: The snake tells it all, with voices. {npc} writes the most popular history ever made, and it is mostly true, and the tortoise, reading a copy years later, finds four things the snake made up and says nothing, because they are the four best bits.

events.text: An immortal envoy of the Jade court, {npc}, travelling ahead of an audit, stops at your river in plain clothes to ask you privately how the other guardians really are. "Off the record," {he} says. The snake points out that there is no such thing, here.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth about each guardian, as you would write it

effects.log: The Dragon, humble and anxious. The Tiger, fair and hungry. The Bird, kind and on fire. The centre, patient as farmland. {npc} listens, and the next audit is the kindest in a thousand years, because it understands what it is auditing.

choices.text: Tell {him} to go and ask them

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "The north is loyal," {he} says, writing it down. "Good. That is the one thing the Jade court was worried about."

events.text: The ending the snake read comes, and you are there: under the window of a physician of the county, ninety, who has saved more lives than anyone in the province and has decided, tonight, not to save one more, because it is hers. Her students are outside the door with every medicine there is.

choices.text: Lie under the window and witness it

effects.log: Her students come in at dawn and find her smiling. You saw it: a long life ended on purpose, by someone who knew exactly what she was doing. The snake reads nothing into it. There is nothing to read. (Write on the Shell: the plate is waiting.)

choices.text: Let the snake whisper the one cure she forgot

effects.log: She remembers it, sits up, takes it, and lives four more years, cross about it. The ending was changed: there is nothing to write. The tortoise says she had decided. The snake says deciding is not dying.

events.text: The ending the snake read comes, and you are there: the last caravan over a mountain pass that a landslide will close tonight for a hundred years. Forty mules, the bells, the drivers singing. You can feel the mountain shifting above them.

choices.text: Watch the last mule cross, and the pass close behind it

effects.log: The last mule is over at midnight. At the first light the mountain comes down across the road with a sound like a drum, and the pass is closed. You saw the crossing end. Nobody died. That was the omen's mercy, not yours. (Write on the Shell: the plate is waiting.)

choices.text: Hold the mountain up one more day for a second caravan

effects.log: You lie against the slope all night and hold it, and a second caravan nobody expected comes through, and then you let go. The ending moved. There is nothing to write, and two villages that would have starved do not.

events.text: The ending the snake read comes, and you are there: an old couple who have quarrelled for fifty years have decided to part, formally, with the elders present, and divide the house down the middle with a rope.

choices.text: Witness the parting

effects.log: They divide the house, the pots, the dog. On the doorstep the old man hands her the better half of the rice without a word, and she takes it without a word. You saw it, every bit. A union broken, and not without love. (Write on the Shell: the plate is waiting.)

choices.text: Let the snake drop the rope in the river

effects.log: Without the rope they cannot agree where the middle is, and argue about it until supper, and eat supper together out of habit, and are still arguing about the middle twenty years later. The ending did not come. The snake is very pleased with itself.

events.text: The ending the snake read comes, and you are there: the funeral of a ferryman on your own river, a man you have held up in floods for forty years. The bier comes down to the water with the bell and the white hemp, and the mourners look at the river as if it should do something.

choices.text: Rise once, and bow both heads as the bier passes

effects.log: The mourners see the river bow. Half of them run. The other half stay and finish the rite, and the ferryman's son pours rice into the water afterwards and says thank you. You saw it all: a man the river loved, buried. (Write on the Shell: the plate is waiting.)

choices.text: Lie still under the water and witness it unseen

effects.log: Nobody sees you. You hear every word of the dirge and the bell and the son's silence. The witnessing is the same either way; the snake says the bowing would have been showing off.

events.text: The ending the snake read comes, and you are there, in the moat of a county yamen: the granary of the county has been emptied by its keeper over twenty years, and tonight the inspectors arrive, and the keeper is setting fire to it to hide the theft, and the fire will take half the town.

choices.text: Witness the granary burn, and the theft come out

effects.log: The fire takes the granary and three streets. In the ashes the inspectors find nothing, and that is the proof. You saw the whole of it, from the moat. A treasury fallen. (Write on the Shell: the plate is waiting.)

choices.text: Put out the fire before it spreads, and let the empty granary speak

effects.log: You come up out of the moat and lie on the burning roof until it goes out, and three streets do not burn. The empty granary is enough for the inspectors. The ending the snake read did not come. Nothing to write; the town is standing.

events.text: The ending the snake read comes, and you are there: a dyke a thousand labourers built, failing in the spring flood exactly where the snake said, and the labourers' camp below it asleep.

choices.text: Witness it go

effects.log: The dyke goes at the third watch. The camp was woken by a dog and is on the hill by the time the water comes. You see every stone of it go. The works ended, and nobody with them. (Write on the Shell: the plate is waiting.)

choices.text: Lie against the breach and hold it till dawn

effects.log: You lie in the breach with the flood on your back all night. At dawn the labourers find a black shell blocking the gap and fill sandbags round it, singing. The dyke holds. The ending was changed; nothing to write; the snake complains of a sore neck for a year.

events.text: The ending the snake read comes, and you are there: a scholar burning his own life's work in his courtyard, a history of the dynasty the new dynasty does not want written. One book at a time, into the brazier.

choices.text: Watch every page burn, and remember them

effects.log: You lie in the courtyard pond and read each page as it curls. By dawn there is nothing left but ash, and the whole history is on your back. You saw a book end. You will never forget it. (Write on the Shell: the plate is waiting.)

choices.text: Let the snake take one book out of the pile while he weeps

effects.log: One book, out of forty, slid away under the snake's coils into the pond. Years later it turns up in a monastery, waterstained, and is copied. The ending was changed, a little. Nothing to write.

events.text: The one the word was for comes down to the water at last: {npc}, old now, older than the one who gave you the word ever got to be. {He} has walked a long way, without knowing why, and stands on the bank looking at the river as if it owed {him} something.

choices.text: Rise, so {he} can see who is bringing it

effects.log: {npc} sees the two heads and is not afraid; some people are not. {He} sits down on the frozen bank to listen. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

choices.text: Let the snake ask {him} first how the years have been

effects.log: Hard, mostly. Some good. {npc} tells it all, to a river, and feels better for it before the word is even said. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

events.text: A word you have carried for years is due, and the one it is for, {npc}, is here, at the ferry steps, with a grandchild. The word is a hard one. The snake has been rehearsing kinder versions all the way down the river, out loud.

choices.text: Tell the snake to stop rehearsing

effects.log: The snake stops, sulking. It will say it as it was given, every word, because the tortoise is watching. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

choices.text: Ask {npc} to send the grandchild away first

effects.log: The grandchild goes off to throw stones at the ice. {npc} turns to the river and waits, very straight, the way people wait for a verdict. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

events.text: The word comes due on the stair of cloud: the one it is for is an immortal now, {npc}, who left the world below long ago and has come to the north edge of the sky to wait, because a dream told {him} to.

choices.text: Ask {him} if {he} remembers the one who gave the word

effects.log: {npc} does, barely: a face, a voice, a winter. "I thought they had forgotten me," {he} says. They had not. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

choices.text: Write the moment on the inside of your shell before you speak

effects.log: The date, the place, the face, waiting. Then the snake lifts its head to speak. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

events.text: Hard frost on the river, and the cracked plate on your back aches the way an old bone does, a dull red glow under the stars that only you can see. The snake pretends not to notice. It always pretends.

choices.text: Turn toward the place of the crack, one journey at least

effects.log: One slow journey toward it, through the frost. You do not get there this year. You are nearer. (-4 health)

choices.text: Ask the snake, plainly, to say what really happened

effects.log: It tells you. It is not much different from what it wrote, and it is completely different. The ache goes on.

choices.text: Lie still and let it ache

effects.log: It aches all winter. In spring it stops, and you forget it, and next frost it will remind you.

events.text: The snake is restless. It has been out of the shell's rim for a month, lying beside you on the riverbed rather than round you, tasting the current from upstream. When you speak to it, it answers late.

choices.text: Talk until it answers on time

effects.log: A season of talking about nothing: the fish, the ferry, a heron with one leg. By the end of it the snake is round the shell again and answering before you have finished the question, which is worse, and better.

choices.text: Give it a task: an omen to read, a word to carry

effects.log: It throws itself into the work like a dog into a river. It is happier with something to do. So, it turns out, is the tortoise.

choices.text: Let it be restless

effects.log: It is restless all year. You lie still all year. Neither of you is happier.

events.text: Diviners' men on the river again, with nets and a sled and a brazier, paid by a court that has heard that the oldest shell in the world is star-plated now, and would read very well indeed.

choices.text: Draw in under the ice

effects.log: They walk over you twice and take you for a rock in the ice. They go home in spring with an ordinary turtle and a story.

choices.text: Let the snake come up through the ice at the first one

effects.log: One black head through the ice at dusk, at eye level. The diviners' men remember urgent business at home.

choices.text: Rise, and let them see the stars on your back

effects.log: They see it: the northern sky lying on the river, breathing. Nobody touches a net. They go home and tell the court there is nothing to be read there that heaven has not already written.

events.text: A traveller on the bank in a flood, with a sick child on their back and the ford gone under brown water. They do not see you. They are looking for a ferry that is not there.

choices.text: Carry them across

effects.log: Something under the water lifts them and carries them, and sets them down on the far bank, and they never see what. The child lives. They tell everybody about the river, and nobody believes them, and they do not care.

choices.text: Let the snake speak to them first, so they are not afraid

effects.log: They are terrified anyway. They climb on anyway. On the far bank the traveller bows to the river and the snake bows back, which they will remember all their lives.
